0.title: Holy Exiles: Living the Gospel Under Pressure
0.overview:
First Peter is the New Testament's sustained theology of exile. Peter writes to Christians scattered across the five provinces of northern Asia Minor — Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia — identifying them with three words that frame everything: elect, resident aliens, of the Dispersion. They are chosen by God and displaced in the world. These two facts stand in permanent tension throughout the letter: you are precious beyond calculation to the God who elected you; you are strangers and foreigners in the world you inhabit. Both are true at the same time, and both must shape how you live.

The recipients were primarily Gentiles — 2:10 quotes Hosea's 'not a people' passage, and 4:3 describes their former lives as pagan. Yet Peter addresses them with the vocabulary of Israel: elect exiles of the Dispersion, a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation. The church has stepped into the covenant identity of Israel and now carries it into a hostile empire. The suffering they face — social ostracism, slander, economic disadvantage, possibly intermittent persecution — is the normal cost of that identity. The letter does not explain why suffering comes; it explains how to endure it and what it means.

The letter's Christological center is 2:21–25 and 3:18–22: Christ's own suffering, death, resurrection, and ascension are the template for Christian existence. He suffered unjustly; he did not retaliate; he entrusted himself to the one who judges justly; he was vindicated. The pattern is not merely an example to follow but a participation to enter: believers share Christ's sufferings (4:13) so that they will share his glory. The theology of suffering in 1 Peter is not stoic endurance but eschatological confidence — the same confidence that carried Jesus through the cross to resurrection is available to every believer in every form of suffering.

The letter was written from 'Babylon' (5:13) — the Jewish-Christian code word for Rome, used also in 4 Ezra and Revelation. Silvanus (Silas) served as secretary, which explains the polished Greek that would be surprising from a Galilean fisherman. The likely date is 62–64 AD, during or shortly before the Neronian persecution that would claim both Peter and Paul.

1.title: Living Hope: Election, Holiness, and the Imperishable Word
1.overview:
The first chapter establishes the theological foundations on which everything else in the letter rests. The opening greeting compresses a full doctrine of election, Trinitarian activity, and covenant identity into two verses. The thanksgiving (vv. 3–12) unfolds the logic of Christian hope: God has given a new birth into a living hope through Christ's resurrection, securing an imperishable inheritance guarded by divine power until the last day. The suffering along the way is not a contradiction of this hope but its testing and confirmation.

The call to holiness (vv. 13–25) follows from the indicative: because you have been born again into this identity, live accordingly. The standard is staggering — 'Be holy, for I am holy' (Lev 11:44) — but the resources match the standard: the same God who demands holiness is the Father who ransomed you at incomprehensible cost. The chapter closes with the word of God as both the instrument of new birth (v. 23) and the only thing that endures when everything else withers (vv. 24–25).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter writes as an apostle to 'elect exiles of the Dispersion' scattered across five provinces of Asia Minor (v.1) — chosen according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, in the sanctification of the Spirit, for obedience to Jesus Christ and for sprinkling with his blood; grace and peace be multiplied to them (v.2).
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Words That Do Not Normally Go Together

Elect is the language of Israel — chosen, God's own. Exiles is parepidemoi, resident foreigners with no standing where they live. Peter sets the highest status beside the lowest and says both are true at once, and the second is not evidence against the first. That is the pastoral problem the whole letter exists to answer: these people were being slandered and excluded, and the natural inference was that God had forgotten them.

Verse 2 is one of the most compressed Trinitarian statements in the New Testament — the Father's foreknowledge as origin, the Spirit's sanctification as means, obedience to Christ and sprinkling with his blood as end. And 'foreknowledge' is not God looking forward to see who would choose him; in biblical usage to know someone is to set your regard on them, as in Amos 3:2, 'you only have I known of all the families of the earth.' It is love fixed beforehand, not information gathered in advance.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The five provinces cover most of modern Turkey, listed in roughly the order a courier would travel them. This is a circular letter, and somebody carried it a very long way. 'Sprinkling with his blood' reaches back to Exodus 24:8, where Moses threw the blood of the covenant over the people — the moment Israel became God's nation.

Now: Peter tells scattered foreigners in Asia Minor that the same thing has happened to them. It is the move he makes throughout the letter: everything said to Israel is applied without adjustment to Gentile converts, because they are now the covenant people — the argument he makes explicitly in 2:9-10.

verseByVerse.quote: Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who are elect exiles of the Dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, in the sanctification of the Spirit, for obedience to Jesus Christ and for sprinkling with his blood: May grace and peace be multiplied to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to those who are elect exiles of the Dispersion.' Two words held together that do not normally belong together, and the whole letter lives in the tension between them.

Elect — chosen, God's own, the language of Israel. Exiles — parepidemoi, resident foreigners, people living somewhere that is not home and who have no standing there. Peter puts the highest possible status beside the lowest and says: both, at once. You are chosen, and you are strangers, and the second is not evidence against the first.

That is the pastoral problem the letter exists to answer. These people were being treated as outsiders — slandered, excluded, in some places worse — and the natural inference was that God had forgotten them. Peter refuses the inference in his first sentence.

The five provinces named — Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, Bithynia — cover most of what is now Turkey, and the order is roughly the route a courier would take, north then clockwise. This is a circular letter, and someone carried it a very long way.

Then verse 2, and it is one of the most compressed Trinitarian statements in the New Testament. According to the foreknowledge of God the Father — the origin. In the sanctification of the Spirit — the means. For obedience to Jesus Christ and for sprinkling with his blood — the end. Three persons, three prepositions, one salvation.

And 'foreknowledge' here is not God peering forward to see who would choose him. In biblical usage to know someone is to set your regard on them — Amos says of Israel, 'you only have I known of all the families of the earth.' It is love fixed beforehand, not information gathered in advance.

'Sprinkling with his blood' reaches back to Exodus 24:8, where Moses took the blood of the covenant and threw it over the people. That is the moment Israel became God's nation. Peter tells scattered foreigners in Asia Minor that the same thing has happened to them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–12 — Born Again to a Living Hope
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Blessed be God, who by his great mercy has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection (v.3), to an inheritance imperishable, undefiled and unfading, kept in heaven (v.4), while we are guarded by God's power through faith for a salvation ready to be revealed (v.5).

In this they rejoice, though grieved for a little while by various trials (v.6), so that the tested genuineness of their faith — more precious than gold refined by fire — may result in praise and glory at the revelation of Jesus Christ (v.7). Though they have not seen him they love him, and rejoice with inexpressible joy filled with glory (v.8), obtaining the outcome of their faith (v.9).

The prophets searched and inquired about this grace (v.10), asking what person or time the Spirit of Christ in them meant when predicting the sufferings and subsequent glories (v.11) — and were told they served not themselves but these readers, in things now announced by the gospel, things angels long to look into (v.12).
verseByVerse.theology:
Kept, and Keeping

The three adjectives describing the inheritance all begin with the same negative letter in Greek — a deliberate triplet: it cannot decay, cannot be polluted, cannot lose its colour. Every one denies something that happens to earthly inheritances, and Peter writes to people whose property had often been taken. The land promised to Israel could be invaded, defiled and lost, and had been.

Then the answering promise. The inheritance is 'kept in heaven for you', and you are 'guarded' — a garrison word, soldiers posted around a city. Both ends of the journey are under guard, and the middle is where the reader currently stands. Note too that the trials come 'if necessary' — not random, not routine, and somebody is deciding.

Verse 8 repays remembering who wrote it. Peter had seen him — pulled nets with him, walked on water toward him, denied him while the man looked at him. Of everyone who could have written 'though you have not seen him, you love him', he is the one for whom it is untrue, and there is no hint of superiority in it. The Lord had already told him where the greater blessing lay (John 20:29).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Verses 10-12 say something extraordinary about inspiration: the prophets studied their own words, trying to work out what they meant. They were not passive dictation machines but readers of what they had written, and what they could not resolve is named exactly — the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories. Both were in the text and the order made no sense until the sequence happened. They were told the answer was not for their generation, and they went on writing.

Now: 'Things into which angels long to look' uses a verb meaning to stoop and peer in — the word used of the disciples bending into the empty tomb. Peter pictures angels leaning over the edge of heaven trying to see. They have never needed redeeming and cannot experience it, and it fascinates them. The gospel these harassed exiles half-understand is the thing angels crane their necks at.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ! According to his great mercy, he has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, to an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you, who by God's power are being guarded through faith for a salvation ready to be revealed in the last time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ!' Peter opens with praise rather than instruction, and the exclamation is in the Greek. Whatever these people were suffering, his first instinct is worship.

'According to his great mercy, he has caused us to be born again.' The verb is anagennao, and Peter is the only New Testament writer who uses it. He had heard the conversation with Nicodemus; he knew what being born again meant before there was a vocabulary for it.

And note the grammar, because it is the point. He caused us. Nobody arranges their own birth, contributes to it, or consents to it in advance. It is the one experience every human being has been entirely passive in, and Peter chose the image deliberately.

'To a living hope.' Not a lively feeling but a hope that is alive — because the one it rests on is. Peter grounds it immediately: 'through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead.' A dead man's promises expire with him. These do not.

Then the inheritance, described with three Greek words that all begin with the same negative letter — a deliberate triplet: imperishable (it cannot decay), undefiled (it cannot be polluted), unfading (it cannot lose its colour).

Every one of those is a denial of something that happens to earthly inheritances, and Peter is writing to people whose property had in many cases been taken. The land promised to Israel could be invaded, defiled and lost, and had been. This one is 'kept in heaven for you' — in the safest possible custody, with your name on it.

And then the answering promise: 'who by God's power are being guarded through faith.' The word is a garrison term — soldiers posted around a city. So the inheritance is kept for you, and you are kept for it. Both ends of the journey are under guard, and the middle is where the reader currently is.

verseByVerse.quote: In this you rejoice, though now for a little while, if necessary, you have been grieved by various trials, so that the tested genuineness of your faith—more precious than gold that perishes though it is tested by fire—may be found to result in praise and glory and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'In this you rejoice' — in what has just been described, not in what is about to be. The joy has an object outside the circumstances, which is the only way it survives the rest of the sentence.

'Though now for a little while, if necessary, you have been grieved by various trials.' Three qualifiers in half a verse, and each is a mercy.

Now — present, and therefore temporary. For a little while — measured against the imperishable inheritance, and Peter has just set the scale. And 'if necessary', which is the tender one: the trials are not random and not routine. They come when there is a reason for them, and somebody is deciding.

Note also that Peter says 'you have been grieved.' He does not pretend the joy cancels the pain or that a Christian should feel less. Both are true at once, and the letter never asks them to choose.

Then the purpose, and the image is a workshop: 'so that the tested genuineness of your faith — more precious than gold that perishes though it is tested by fire — may be found to result in praise and glory and honour.'

The word is the assayer's: what is left when the fire has taken everything else. And the comparison is exact rather than decorative. Gold is refined by fire and is still perishable; faith is refined the same way and is not. So the process is identical and the product is worth more, which is Peter's answer to a suffering congregation asking what any of this is for.

And see where the praise lands: 'at the revelation of Jesus Christ.' Not now. The vindication is on a date, and the letter keeps pointing to it — which is what makes 'for a little while' bearable rather than glib.

verseByVerse.quote: Though you have not seen him, you love him. Though you do not now see him, you believe in him and rejoice with joy that is inexpressible and filled with glory, obtaining the outcome of your faith, the salvation of your souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Though you have not seen him, you love him.' Stop on that, and remember who is writing it.

Peter had seen him. He had pulled nets with him, walked on water toward him, watched him transfigured, and denied him in a courtyard while the man looked at him. Of all the people who could have written this sentence, he is the one for whom it is not true.

And there is no hint of superiority in it. He does not say 'you have not seen him as I did.' He states their position and honours it, and the Lord had already told him where the greater blessing lay: 'blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed' (John 20:29).

'Though you do not now see him, you believe in him and rejoice with joy that is inexpressible and filled with glory.' Two adjectives, and both are reaching past the end of language.

Inexpressible means it cannot be said — Peter, describing their joy, admits he has no words for it. And 'filled with glory' most likely means the glory of the age to come has already leaked into it. This is not cheerfulness. It is a foretaste, arriving in people whose lives were hard.

'Obtaining the outcome of your faith, the salvation of your souls.' The word means the end, what a thing arrives at. And the present tense matters: not 'you will obtain' but you are obtaining, now, in the middle of the trials. The salvation is being received while the grief of verse 6 is still going on.

verseByVerse.quote: Concerning this salvation, the prophets who prophesied about the grace that was to be yours searched and inquired carefully, inquiring what person or time the Spirit of Christ in them was indicating when he predicted the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories. It was revealed to them that they were serving not themselves but you, in the things that have now been announced to you through those who preached the good news to you by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven, things into which angels long to look.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter now does something remarkable: he tells a small, harassed congregation of foreigners that they are the point of the entire Old Testament.

'The prophets who prophesied about the grace that was to be yours searched and inquired carefully.' Two verbs, both intensive. The men who wrote Scripture studied their own words, trying to work out what they meant — which is an extraordinary thing to be told about inspiration. They were not passive dictation machines. They were readers of what they had written, and puzzled by it.

'Inquiring what person or time the Spirit of Christ in them was indicating.' Note 'the Spirit of Christ in them' — Peter says the prophets were carrying the Spirit of a Christ not yet born.

And what they could not resolve is named exactly: 'the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories.' Both were there in the text, and the order made no sense — a suffering figure and a glorified one. Two Messiahs, or one in sequence? Nobody could tell until the sequence happened.

'It was revealed to them that they were serving not themselves but you.' They were told, in effect, that the answer was not for their generation. And they went on writing. Anyone labouring at something whose usefulness they will not live to see is in very good company.

Then the last clause, and it is one of the most arresting in the New Testament: 'things into which angels long to look.'

The verb means to stoop down and peer in — it is used of the disciples bending to look into the empty tomb. Peter pictures the angels leaning over the edge of heaven, trying to see. They have never needed redeeming and cannot experience it, and it fascinates them. The gospel these exiles half-understand is the thing angels crane their necks at.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–25 — Be Holy, for I Am Holy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Therefore gird up the loins of your mind, be sober-minded, and set your hope fully on the grace coming at the revelation of Jesus Christ (v.13). As obedient children, do not be conformed to the passions of your former ignorance (v.14), but as he who called you is holy, be holy in all your conduct (v.15), since it is written, 'You shall be holy, for I am holy' (v.16).

If you call on him as Father who judges impartially, conduct yourselves with fear throughout your exile (v.17) — knowing you were ransomed from the futile ways inherited from your forefathers, not with silver or gold (v.18) but with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish (v.19), foreknown before the foundation of the world and made manifest in the last times for your sake (v.20), who through him believe in God, who raised him and gave him glory, so that your faith and hope are in God (v.21).

Having purified your souls by obedience to the truth for sincere brotherly love, love one another earnestly from a pure heart (v.22), since you have been born again of imperishable seed through the living and abiding word of God (v.23) — for all flesh is grass and its glory the flower of grass, which withers and falls (v.24), but the word of the Lord remains forever, and that word is the gospel preached to you (v.25).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Fear of a Child

Verse 17 puts 'Father' and 'judges impartially' in one sentence, which modern readers tend to hold apart. The word for impartial is literally without receiving the face — God does not defer to appearance, position or connection. That is terrifying to those with advantages and profoundly good news to people at the bottom of every social ladder in Asia Minor.

And the 'fear' commanded is not terror of condemnation — Peter has just said Father. It is the reverence of someone who knows exactly who he is dealing with. A useful test: fear that drives you away from God is the wrong kind; fear that keeps you careful in his presence is the right one. A child who is not frightened of his father may still not be casual with him. And a man who genuinely fears God has very little capacity left for fearing anybody else, which is the practical liberation this letter keeps offering.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: 'Preparing your minds for action' translates a vivid idiom — girding up the loins of the mind. A man in a long robe pulled it up and tucked it into his belt before he could run or work, or he would trip. There may also be a memory of the first Passover, eaten with loins girded, ready to leave Egypt at short notice. And the quotation in verse 16 is from Leviticus 11:44, spoken to Israel at Sinai and applied by Peter without adjustment to Gentile converts in Bithynia.

Now: Note the word 'inherited' in verse 18. The futile ways came down to these readers; they did not choose them. Peter is describing what almost nobody escapes by deciding to — the handed-down apparatus of how your family has always done things — which is precisely why a ransom was needed rather than advice. And the price sets the value: for people being treated as worthless, you may work out what something is valued at by looking at what was paid for it. Isaiah 40, quoted at the end, was itself written to exiles wondering whether God had finished with them, and it opens 'comfort, comfort my people.'

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, preparing your minds for action, and being sober-minded, set your hope fully on the grace that will be brought to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Therefore' — and everything from here rests on the twelve verses behind it. Peter never gives a command until he has given a reason.

'Preparing your minds for action' translates a vivid Greek idiom: girding up the loins of your mind. A man in that world wore a long robe, and before he could run, fight or work he pulled it up and tucked it into his belt. Otherwise he would trip.

Applied to the mind, it means gathering up whatever is loose and trailing. Peter is not asking for more feeling; he is asking for mental discipline — the deliberate collecting of a mind that would otherwise flap about. There may also be a memory in it of the first Passover, eaten with loins girded, ready to leave Egypt at short notice.

'And being sober-minded.' The word is literally the opposite of drunk, and it means clear-headed, unintoxicated, seeing things as they are. Peter uses it three times in this short letter. Suffering distorts judgement, and so does fear, and so does the surrounding culture's version of reality.

Then the command itself, and both halves matter: 'set your hope fully on the grace that will be brought to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ.'

Fully — completely, without reserve, with nothing held back for a second option. Hope is being treated here as something you place, deliberately, in one location. And the location is not what God will do for them next year but what will be brought when Christ appears.

Which is a demanding instruction for people who would have preferred relief now. Peter does not promise the trials will stop. He tells them where to put their hope so that it is not destroyed if they do not.

verseByVerse.quote: As obedient children, do not be conformed to the passions of your former ignorance, but as he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct, since it is written, "You shall be holy, for I am holy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'As obedient children' — literally children of obedience, a Hebrew way of saying obedience characterises them. It is what they are made of, not merely what they do.

'Do not be conformed to the passions of your former ignorance.' The verb means to be shaped from outside, pressed into a mould — the same word Paul uses in Romans 12:2. The pressure is constant and it is not usually noticed, which is why it has to be resisted deliberately.

'Your former ignorance' tells us these readers were largely Gentiles. And it is a merciful description of a pagan past: not wickedness but not-knowing. They behaved that way because they did not know any better, and now they do.

Then the standard, and it is startling: 'as he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct.' The measure is not an improvement on the surrounding culture, nor the best available human example. It is God himself.

Holiness means set apart, other, belonging to a different order — and applied to conduct it means a life that is visibly not from around here. Which is exactly the letter's theme: exiles behave like citizens of the place they are from.

'In all your conduct' closes the loophole everyone reaches for. Not in religious matters, not in public, not on the parts of life that show. All of it.

Then the quotation, from Leviticus 11:44, and Peter is doing something bold with it. That command was given to Israel at Sinai, and he applies it without adjustment to Gentile converts in Bithynia. What was said to the covenant nation is now said to them, because they are the covenant people — which is the argument he will make explicitly in chapter 2.

verseByVerse.quote: And if you call on him as Father who judges impartially according to each one's deeds, conduct yourselves with fear throughout the time of your exile,
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And if you call on him as Father' — and the 'if' is not a doubt but a given: since you do. Peter grants them the most intimate name available.

And then, in the same breath, 'who judges impartially according to each one's deeds.' The two halves sit oddly together for modern readers, who tend to hold Father and Judge apart. Peter does not.

The word for impartial is the one from James 2 — literally without receiving the face. God does not defer to appearance, position or connection, and Peter is telling that to people at the bottom of every social ladder in Asia Minor. Impartiality is terrifying to those with advantages and profoundly good news to those with none.

'Conduct yourselves with fear throughout the time of your exile.' This needs care, because the same letter says perfect love casts out fear is elsewhere in the New Testament, and Peter is not contradicting it. The fear here is not terror of condemnation — he has just called God Father. It is the reverence of someone who knows exactly who he is dealing with.

A useful test of the difference: fear that drives you away from God is the wrong kind, and fear that keeps you careful in his presence is the right one. A child who is not frightened of his father may still not be casual with him.

'Throughout the time of your exile.' The exile word again from verse 1, and now with a duration attached. It has a beginning and an end, and they are living inside it. Peter's counsel for the whole stretch is one word: reverence — because a man who genuinely fears God has very little capacity left for fearing anybody else, which is the practical liberation this letter keeps offering.

verseByVerse.quote: knowing that you were ransomed from the futile ways inherited from your forefathers, not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Knowing that you were ransomed' — and the participle explains the fear of verse 17. Reverence rests on knowledge of what was paid.

The word is the slave-market and the prisoner-exchange word: a price handed over to secure a release. And it carries the exodus behind it, where God ransomed Israel out of Egypt — the event this whole passage keeps gesturing at.

'From the futile ways inherited from your forefathers.' That is a striking thing to say to Gentile readers, and it names what most of them would have called their heritage. Futile means empty, achieving nothing — the standard biblical verdict on idols.

And 'inherited' is the sharp word. These ways came down to them; they did not choose them. Peter is describing something almost nobody escapes by deciding to — the whole handed-down apparatus of how your family has always done things, which is precisely why a ransom was needed rather than advice.

'Not with perishable things such as silver or gold.' Peter names the two most durable currencies in the ancient world and calls them perishable. He has already used gold as the standard of value in verse 7 and found it wanting there too.

'But with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot.' The Passover lamb had to be inspected and found flawless before it could be used. Peter, who heard John the Baptist say 'behold, the Lamb of God', applies the inspection language to Christ — and the price is set by what was spent, not by what the readers thought they were worth.

Which is the pastoral force of it for people being treated as worthless. You may work out what something is valued at by looking at what was paid for it.

verseByVerse.quote: He was foreknown before the foundation of the world but was made manifest in the last times for the sake of you who through him are believers in God, who raised him from the dead and gave him glory, so that your faith and hope are in God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'He was foreknown before the foundation of the world.' The word is the same one used of the readers in verse 2 — Christ and his people are both foreknown, and the parallel is not accidental.

'Before the foundation of the world' means before there was a world to fall. The cross was not God's response to an emergency, improvised after things went wrong. The Lamb was in view before Genesis 1.

'But was made manifest in the last times' — the hidden purpose stepping into history at a date. And 'the last times' is the New Testament's standard description of the period the readers are in: the final era began at Bethlehem, and everything since is its outworking.

'For the sake of you.' Peter puts it as bluntly as it can be put. The eternal purpose, hidden before the world was made, was manifested for the sake of a scattered group of foreigners in Pontus and Bithynia who were being slandered by their neighbours.

'Who through him are believers in God.' Even their faith arrives by way of Christ. He is not merely the object of it but the route to it.

'Who raised him from the dead and gave him glory, so that your faith and hope are in God.' Note the logic of the last clause. The resurrection is not offered here primarily as proof of an event but as the ground of a disposition — God did that, therefore your faith and hope can rest on him. It is the same argument as verse 3, and Peter has now made it twice in twenty verses. A man who raises the dead can be trusted with an inheritance.

verseByVerse.quote: Having purified your souls by your obedience to the truth for a sincere brotherly love, love one another earnestly from a pure heart,
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Having purified your souls by your obedience to the truth.' The purification is stated as accomplished — it has happened. And the means is obedience to the truth, which for Peter means the gospel believed and acted on rather than a code kept.

And note what it produced: 'for a sincere brotherly love.' The purifying had an aim, and the aim was other people. Sincere is anypokritos — un-play-acted, without the mask. Peter allows that love can be performed, and rules it out.

Then the command, and after that description it might have seemed unnecessary: 'love one another earnestly from a pure heart.'

That is the pattern the New Testament always follows. You have been purified for love; therefore love. The indicative first, then the imperative — and the imperative is needed precisely because what is true of us is not yet automatic in us.

'Earnestly' is the interesting word. It means stretched out, strained, at full extent — used of a muscle under tension and of an athlete's effort. Peter is not asking for warm feeling but for love that costs something to sustain.

Which is realistic about what he is asking. These were scattered congregations of people thrown together by nothing except Christ — different races, classes and households, with slaves and masters in the same room. Loving that group was not going to happen by temperament. It was going to take the sort of effort the word describes.

verseByVerse.quote: since you have been born again, not of perishable seed but of imperishable, through the living and abiding word of God;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter now gives the reason underneath the command, and it takes him back to verse 3: 'since you have been born again.'

The logic is family. Love one another — because you have the same birth. They are brothers by regeneration, not by preference, and that is why the love is commanded rather than left to affinity. You do not choose your siblings.

'Not of perishable seed but of imperishable.' There is that word again — the third time in the chapter. The inheritance is imperishable (v.4), the ransom was not paid in perishable silver (v.18), and now the seed itself is imperishable. Peter is building a single case for readers whose visible world was all too perishable.

Natural birth uses seed that dies; everyone in that congregation had buried somebody. This birth does not, which means the family it creates cannot be dissolved by the thing that dissolves every other family.

'Through the living and abiding word of God.' The seed is the word — the parable of the sower is not far away, and Peter had heard it explained.

And both adjectives are doing work. Living: it is not inert information but something with life in it, which is why it can generate life. Abiding: it remains, which is the point the quotation in the next verse will drive home. The word that gave them birth is the one thing in their situation that will still be there when everything visible has gone.

verseByVerse.quote: for "All flesh is like grass and all its glory like the flower of grass. The grass withers, and the flower falls, but the word of the Lord remains forever." And this word is the good news that was preached to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter closes the chapter with Isaiah 40:6-8, and the choice of passage is deliberate. Isaiah 40 was written to exiles — people far from home, wondering whether God had finished with them. It opens 'comfort, comfort my people.'

'All flesh is like grass and all its glory like the flower of grass. The grass withers, and the flower falls.' The picture is the one James used: the hills green after the rains, and the desert wind browning the whole landscape within a day.

And note that it is not only the grass but 'all its glory' — the flower, the impressive part. Peter is writing to people being outclassed and outranked by neighbours with standing, and Isaiah's word is that the standing is the most temporary thing about them. Not merely human life but human splendour is what withers.

'But the word of the Lord remains forever.' The single contrast, and everything in the chapter has been arranged to arrive here. Set the imperishable seed beside the withering flower and you have Peter's whole estimate of the situation.

Then the last line, and it is the one that lands: 'And this word is the good news that was preached to you.'

Isaiah's eternal word is not a distant abstraction. It is the specific message somebody brought to Pontus and Cappadocia and said out loud in a room — the thing these readers heard, perhaps from a travelling trader, and believed.

That is a remarkable dignity to confer on ordinary preaching. The word that outlasts all flesh and every human glory is the same word an unnamed evangelist spoke to a handful of foreigners, and it is the seed that gave them a birth that cannot perish.

2.title: Living Stones and Holy Exiles: Identity, Witness, and the Suffering Christ
2.overview: Chapter 2 moves from the foundations of Christian identity (vv. 1–10) to its outworking in a hostile world (vv. 11–25). The two movements are inseparable: you are living stones in God's temple, a chosen race, a royal priesthood — therefore, conduct yourselves among the Gentiles with such good works that those who slander you will glorify God. Identity produces conduct; conduct commends identity. The chapter's climax is the extended meditation on Christ's unjust suffering (vv. 18–25), which frames the household code not as social conformity but as participation in the pattern of the suffering Servant.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Living Stones, a Royal Priesthood
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Put away malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy and slander (v.1); like newborn infants crave the pure spiritual milk, to grow up into salvation (v.2), if you have tasted that the Lord is good (v.3). Coming to him, a living stone rejected by men but chosen and precious to God (v.4), you yourselves as living stones are being built into a spiritual house, a holy priesthood offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable through Jesus Christ (v.5).

For Scripture says God lays in Zion a chosen and precious cornerstone, and whoever believes will not be put to shame (v.6). So the honour is for believers; but for unbelievers the stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone (v.7), and a stone of stumbling — they stumble because they disobey the word (v.8). But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, to proclaim the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvellous light (v.9). Once not a people, now God's people; once without mercy, now shown mercy (v.10).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Priesthood of All Believers

Verse 5 is the root of what the Reformers meant by that phrase, and it repays seeing how thoroughly it dismantles the old arrangement. The temple had a building, a priesthood and sacrifices, and ordinary people had access to none of the three. Peter tells a scattered congregation that they are the building, they are the priesthood, and they offer the sacrifices. The last three words keep it from becoming self-important: acceptable to God 'through Jesus Christ' — even a priesthood's offerings need a mediator.

The four titles in verse 9 are lifted straight from what God said to Israel at Sinai (Exod 19:5-6; Isa 43:20; Deut 7:6), and Peter hands them without qualification to Gentile converts in Asia Minor — people with no race worth naming, no priesthood, no nation and no possessions worth the word.

Verse 8's hard clause repays care. Peter gives the reason for the stumbling first, and it is disobedience — a real refusal, genuinely theirs. The 'destined' clause attaches most naturally to the stumbling that follows such disobedience, not to the disobedience itself. Scripture consistently holds both God's sovereignty over the outcome and full human responsibility for the refusal, and it will not do to soften either half.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The five sins of verse 1 have one thing in common — every one is against other people, and four are committed with words or with a face. Peter has just commanded earnest love from a pure heart (1:22), and this is the list of what makes that impossible. Note especially slander, which was exactly what these readers were suffering from outside (2:12): he will not let a congregation being slandered do to each other what is being done to them.

Now: Peter's use of 'milk' differs from Paul's and the difference matters. In 1 Corinthians 3 milk is the beginner's diet, contrasted with solid food; here it is not a stage to outgrow but the food that produces growth — 'that by it you may grow up into salvation.' The goal is maturity and the diet does not change. And verse 10 is Hosea: the prophet was told to name his children Not-My-People and No-Mercy as living signs of God's verdict, then promised the names would be reversed. Peter applies the reversal to people who never bore the names — whatever they are being called in Pontus, their name has already been changed once.

verseByVerse.quote: So put away all malice and all deceit and hypocrisy and envy and all slander. Like newborn infants, long for the pure spiritual milk, that by it you may grow up into salvation— if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So put away' — the verb is the one for stripping off clothing, and the 'so' ties it to the new birth of 1:23. These are the garments of the old family, and they no longer fit.

Look at the five items, because they have one thing in common: malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy, slander. Every one is a sin against other people, and four of the five are done with words or with a face. Peter has just commanded earnest love from a pure heart (1:22); this is the list of what makes that impossible.

Note especially hypocrisy — the actor's mask — set beside sincere love in 1:22, which is the same word negated. And slander, which was exactly what these readers were suffering from outside (2:12). Peter will not let a congregation being slandered do to each other what is being done to them.

'Like newborn infants, long for the pure spiritual milk.' The image follows the birth: newly born people should have an appetite. And the verb is strong — crave, yearn for — the noise a hungry baby makes, which is not a polite request.

'Spiritual milk' translates a word related to logos; the milk is the word that gave them birth (1:23). And 'pure' is the opposite of the deceit just named — unadulterated, nothing mixed in.

Peter's use of milk is worth noting because it differs from Paul's. In 1 Corinthians 3 milk is the beginner's diet, contrasted with solid food. Here it is not a stage to be outgrown but the food that produces growth: 'that by it you may grow up into salvation.' The goal is maturity, and the diet does not change.

'If indeed you have tasted that the Lord is good' quotes Psalm 34:8, a psalm Peter draws on repeatedly in this letter. And the argument is from experience: an appetite follows a taste. People who have genuinely tasted something good do not need to be persuaded to want more of it.

verseByVerse.quote: As you come to him, a living stone rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen and precious, you yourselves like living stones are being built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The metaphor changes from infancy to masonry, and Peter builds a whole doctrine of the church out of one word.

'As you come to him, a living stone.' The phrase is a deliberate paradox — stone is the deadest material there is, and Peter attaches the word he has been using of hope (1:3) and the word of God (1:23). A stone that is alive.

'Rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen and precious.' There is the letter's whole theme in one line, and it is applied first to Christ. Two verdicts on the same person, running in opposite directions — and the readers, rejected in Pontus and Bithynia, are being told which verdict counts.

'You yourselves like living stones are being built up as a spiritual house.' The passive matters: they are being built. Not building themselves, and not assembling by choice. Someone is doing it, and stones do not select their neighbours in a wall.

And the singular is the point. Not houses but a house — one structure. A stone on its own is rubble; it becomes masonry only by being set against other stones. Peter is writing to scattered, isolated believers and telling them they are load-bearing parts of one building.

'To be a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices.' This is the root of what the Reformers called the priesthood of all believers, and note how thoroughly it dismantles the old arrangement. In the temple there was a building, a priesthood and sacrifices, and ordinary people had access to none of them. Peter says the congregation is the building, is the priesthood, and offers the sacrifices.

And the last three words keep it from being self-important: acceptable to God 'through Jesus Christ.' Even the offerings of a priesthood need a mediator.

verseByVerse.quote: For it stands in Scripture: "Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone, a cornerstone chosen and precious, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame." So the honor is for you who believe, but for those who do not believe, "The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone," and "A stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense." They stumble because they disobey the word, as they were destined to do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter now stacks three stone texts from the Old Testament, and the effect is cumulative: this was always how it was going to go.

The first is Isaiah 28:16: 'Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone, a cornerstone chosen and precious, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame.' The cornerstone was the stone that set the lines of the whole building — every wall was measured from it. And 'will not be put to shame' is exactly the promise a slandered congregation needed.

The second is Psalm 118:22: 'The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.' The Lord had quoted this of himself (Matt 21:42), and Peter had quoted it before the Sanhedrin (Acts 4:11) — to the very builders who had done the rejecting. He has been preaching this text for thirty years.

The third is Isaiah 8:14: 'A stone of stumbling, and a rock of offence.' And here the images collide deliberately. The same stone is a foundation to some and an obstacle to others. Nothing about the stone changes; what differs is whether a man builds on it or trips over it.

Then the hard sentence: 'They stumble because they disobey the word, as they were destined to do.'

Read the order carefully, because it is often reversed. Peter gives the reason for the stumbling first, and it is disobedience — a real refusal, genuinely theirs. The destining clause attaches most naturally to the stumbling that follows such disobedience, not to the disobedience itself. Scripture consistently holds both: God's sovereignty over the outcome, and full human responsibility for the refusal.

And it will not do to soften either half. Peter has already said these readers were chosen according to foreknowledge (1:2); he is not going to pretend the other side of that is nothing. What he does not do is make God the author of the disobedience.

verseByVerse.quote: But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, that you may proclaim the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light. Once you were not a people, but now you are God's people; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But you' — and the contrast with the stumblers is total. Four titles follow, and every one is lifted straight out of what God said to Israel at Sinai.

'A chosen race' (Isa 43:20). 'A royal priesthood' and 'a holy nation' (Exod 19:6). 'A people for his own possession' (Exod 19:5; Deut 7:6). Peter takes the constitutional documents of Israel and hands them, without qualification, to Gentile converts in Asia Minor.

Consider what it would have meant to hear that read aloud. These were people with no race worth naming, no priesthood, no nation, and no possessions worth the word. Peter tells them they are all four.

And the purpose is stated: 'that you may proclaim the excellencies of him who called you.' The word means to tell out, to publish. A priesthood exists to represent God to people and people to God, and Peter gives the whole congregation the job.

'Out of darkness into his marvellous light.' A conversion described as a relocation — and it echoes the exodus again, out of Egypt and into the land.

Then verse 10, which is Hosea, and it is the tenderest thing in the chapter: 'Once you were not a people, but now you are God's people; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.'

Hosea was commanded to name his children Not-My-People and No-Mercy, as living signs of God's verdict on Israel — and then promised that the names would be reversed (Hos 1:6-10; 2:23). Peter applies the reversal to Gentiles who never had the names in the first place, and the sentence structure carries it: once… now, twice over. Whatever these readers are being called in Pontus, their name has already been changed once.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–25 — Submission, and the Steps of Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
As sojourners and exiles, abstain from the passions of the flesh, which wage war against the soul (v.11); keep your conduct among the Gentiles honourable, so that those who slander you may see your good deeds and glorify God (v.12). Be subject for the Lord's sake to every human institution — the emperor (v.13) and his governors, sent to punish evil and praise good (v.14) — for by doing good you muzzle the ignorance of foolish people (v.15). Live as free people, not using freedom as a cover-up for evil, but as servants of God (v.16). Honour everyone; love the brotherhood; fear God; honour the emperor (v.17).

Servants, be subject to your masters with all respect, not only the gentle but also the unjust (v.18); for it is grace when, mindful of God, one endures unjust suffering (v.19) — there is no credit in enduring a deserved beating, but there is in an undeserved one (v.20). To this you were called, since Christ suffered for you, leaving a copybook line to trace (v.21). He committed no sin, nor was deceit in his mouth (v.22); reviled, he did not revile back; suffering, he did not threaten, but kept entrusting himself to him who judges justly (v.23). He bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness; by his wounds you were healed (v.24). You were straying like sheep, and have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls (v.25).
verseByVerse.theology:
Entrusting Rather Than Suppressing

Verse 23 supplies the mechanism without which this passage would be cruel. Christ 'kept entrusting himself to him who judges justly' — the verb means to hand over or deposit, and it is continuous: again and again, through the trial and the flogging and the nails. He was not suppressing the desire for justice; he was transferring it. The case was not dropped, it was handed to a judge who would hear it properly.

That is precisely what a slave with no court can do, and it is why Peter can ask this of people with no other recourse. Note too that 'did not threaten' is the telling detail: a threat is the last weapon of someone who has run out of others, and Christ uniquely was not out of options — he could have called twelve legions of angels, and said so.

Then verse 24 steps decisively past example into substitution, which no follower can imitate. 'The tree' is not poetic language for the cross but the term from Deuteronomy 21:23 — cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree — and it is Peter's settled way of preaching the cross (Acts 5:30; 10:39).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter addresses slaves directly, as moral agents with choices to make. No Greek or Roman moralist did that; slaves were tools, and you addressed their owners. The mere existence of the sentence assumes a dignity the culture denied. And the emperor of verse 13 was almost certainly Nero, who within a few years would use Christians as torches in his gardens and under whom Peter himself would die — so this is not submission made conditional on good government. The limits exist and Peter knew them: it was he who told the Sanhedrin 'we must obey God rather than men' (Acts 5:29).

Now: Look at what verse 17 does with four commands in eight words. The emperor receives the same verb as everyone else — honour, the identical word — and does not receive the verb reserved for God. In a world where emperors were called divine and incense was burned to them, that is a carefully calibrated sentence: Caesar is worth exactly as much honour as the man who cleans his stables, and not one degree of the fear that belongs to God. And the 'example' of verse 21 is hypogrammos — the schoolmaster's copybook line written at the top of the page for a child to trace underneath. Peter, who said he would follow to prison and death and did not, chose that image; he knows exactly how hard tracing those letters is.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, I urge you as sojourners and exiles to abstain from the passions of the flesh, which wage war against your soul. Keep your conduct among the Gentiles honorable, so that when they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day of visitation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Beloved, I urge you as sojourners and exiles.' The two words from 1:1 and 1:17 return together, and Peter uses them as the ground of the ethics that follow. Behave like what you are.

'To abstain from the passions of the flesh, which wage war against your soul.' The military image is deliberate in a letter about outside hostility. Peter has spent two chapters on what the neighbours are doing; here he names a nearer enemy, and it is inside the walls.

That is a genuinely important pastoral point. A community under external pressure naturally locates all its danger outside, and Peter will not let them. The passions of the flesh are conducting a campaign, and it is against the very soul whose salvation he has just described.

Then the outward face of the same holiness: 'Keep your conduct among the Gentiles honourable.' The word means beautiful, attractive — not merely correct but winsome. And 'among the Gentiles' is striking, since most of these readers were Gentiles; Peter has so thoroughly reclassified them as Israel that their old category is now the outsiders' name.

'So that when they speak against you as evildoers' — not if. The slander is assumed. Christians were accused of atheism for refusing the gods, of cannibalism for the Lord's Supper, and of disloyalty for confessing another Lord.

'They may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day of visitation.' The strategy is not argument but visibility, and Peter expects the slander to be defeated by the evidence of ordinary life. It is his Lord's own instruction (Matt 5:16) — and the man writing had heard it on the hillside.

verseByVerse.quote: Be subject for the Lord's sake to every human institution, whether it be to the emperor as supreme, or to governors as sent by him to punish those who do evil and to praise those who do good. For this is the will of God, that by doing good you should put to silence the ignorance of foolish people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Be subject for the Lord's sake to every human institution.' And the first three words carry the whole weight: for the Lord's sake. Not because the state deserves it, not because it is competent, but because he requires it.

Remember who the emperor was. This letter was most likely written in the early 60s, which means the man 'as supreme' was Nero — who within a few years would be using Christians as torches in his gardens, and under whom Peter himself would almost certainly die.

That fact should govern how the verse is read. Peter is not describing an ideal government or making submission conditional on good behaviour. He is telling a persecuted minority to be model subjects of a ruler who will kill them.

'Or to governors as sent by him to punish those who do evil and to praise those who do good.' The stated function is justice — and Peter, who had been flogged by such authorities and would be executed by them, states it anyway. He is describing the office rather than flattering the officeholders.

The limits are not spelled out here, but they exist and Peter knew them: it was he who told the Sanhedrin, 'we must obey God rather than men' (Acts 5:29). Submission is the settled posture; it is not unconditional, and where the state commands what God forbids the same apostle disobeyed and took the beating.

Then the reason: 'that by doing good you should put to silence the ignorance of foolish people.' The verb means to muzzle. The best answer to slander is a life that makes it obviously untrue, and Peter's strategy is not to win the argument but to remove its material.

verseByVerse.quote: Live as people who are free, not using your freedom as a cover-up for evil, but living as servants of God. Honor everyone. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the emperor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Live as people who are free.' It is an extraordinary thing to say to a group he has just told to submit to Nero — and to slaves, two verses later. Peter's category of freedom is evidently not political.

'Not using your freedom as a cover-up for evil.' The word means a veil or cloak, something thrown over what is underneath. The abuse is perennial: liberty in Christ invoked as permission, and Peter names it before anyone can try it.

'But living as servants of God.' Free, and slaves — and the paradox is the resolution rather than the problem. A man wholly owned by God is beyond the reach of anyone else's ownership, which is precisely why a Christian slave in verse 18 can be told he is free.

Then four commands in eight words, and the arrangement repays attention.

'Honour everyone.' Universal, and it comes first. Every human being is to be given honour — which in a rigidly stratified society was close to revolutionary.

'Love the brotherhood.' A narrower circle and a warmer word. The family gets love, not merely honour.

'Fear God.' Reverence, and it belongs to one being only.

'Honour the emperor.' And now look at what Peter has done. The emperor gets the same verb as everyone — honour, the identical word as the first command — and he does not get the verb reserved for God. In a world where emperors were being called divine and incense was burned to them, that is a carefully calibrated sentence. Caesar is worth exactly as much honour as the man who cleans his stables, and not one degree of the fear that belongs to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Servants, be subject to your masters with all respect, not only to the good and gentle but also to the unjust. For this is a gracious thing, when, mindful of God, one endures sorrows while suffering unjustly. For what credit is it if, when you sin and are beaten for it, you endure? But if when you do good and suffer for it you endure, this is a gracious thing in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Servants, be subject to your masters with all respect.' The word is oiketai, household slaves — and it should be said plainly that these were slaves, not employees, and that perhaps a third of the population of those cities was enslaved.

Note first who is being addressed. Peter speaks to slaves directly, as moral agents with choices to make. No Greek or Roman moralist did that; slaves were tools, and you addressed their owners. The mere fact of the sentence assumes a dignity the culture denied.

And note what is not here. Peter gives no corresponding instruction to masters, as Paul does — most likely because these congregations had few or none. He is writing to the bottom of the ladder.

'Not only to the good and gentle but also to the unjust.' There is the hard part, and Peter does not pretend otherwise. The word for unjust means crooked, bent — unreasonable people, and the household slave had no appeal against one.

Then the principle, stated twice: 'this is a gracious thing, when, mindful of God, one endures sorrows while suffering unjustly.' The phrase is literally this is grace — the same word as God's favour. Something of God's own grace is present in that endurance.

And the qualifier is essential: 'mindful of God'. What makes it grace is not the suffering, which by itself is merely misfortune, but that the sufferer is thinking about God while it happens. Peter is not commending endurance as a virtue in the abstract; he is describing a man who takes the injustice and holds God in view through it.

'For what credit is it if, when you sin and are beaten for it, you endure?' The distinction is drawn sharply, and it protects the teaching from being sentimental. Deserved trouble borne quietly is not a spiritual achievement. The grace is in the undeserved kind.

verseByVerse.quote: For to this you have been called, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his steps.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'For to this you have been called.' Stop there, because it is one of the most difficult sentences in the New Testament. Called — to unjust suffering.

Peter does not say suffering is inevitable, or that God will bring good out of it, though both are true elsewhere. He says it is what they were called to, using the same word he has used of their calling out of darkness into marvellous light (2:9). One calling, two faces.

'Because Christ also suffered for you.' And there is the reason. The pattern is not arbitrary; it is his. A servant who suffers unjustly is not outside the will of God but walking where his Lord walked.

'Leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his steps.' The word for example is hypogrammos — and it is beautifully concrete. It is the schoolmaster's copybook line: the letters written at the top of the page for a child to trace underneath. Peter's picture of discipleship is a child's hand moving over the master's letters.

'Follow in his steps' keeps the same idea — footprints to be trodden in, one at a time.

And Peter, of all people, chose that image. He is the man who said he would follow to prison and to death, and did not, and whose restoration on the beach ended with 'follow me' (John 21:19). He knows exactly how hard tracing those letters is, and he is writing to slaves rather than to apostles.

verseByVerse.quote: He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What follows is one of the most sustained meditations on Isaiah 53 in the New Testament, and Peter applies it, astonishingly, as workplace instruction for slaves.

'He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth' is Isaiah 53:9 almost verbatim. And the relevance to the readers is exact: a slave suffering unjustly is tempted above all to the two things named — retaliation, and the small deceits by which the powerless survive.

Then verse 23, and Peter is describing something he watched: 'When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten.'

He was in the courtyard. He heard the mockery, and he was close enough to see the face it was aimed at. The imperfect tenses in Greek suggest sustained action — it kept coming, and the silence kept holding.

'Did not threaten' is the telling one, because a threat is the last weapon of somebody who has run out of others. And Christ, uniquely, was not out of options: he could have called twelve legions of angels and said so.

Then the positive, and this is the hinge of the whole passage: 'but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly.' The verb means to hand over, to deposit — and it is continuous. Not once, but again and again, through the trial and the flogging and the nails.

And that is the mechanism, which the passage would be cruel without. He was not suppressing the desire for justice; he was transferring it. The case was not dropped — it was handed to a judge who would hear it properly. Which is precisely what a slave with no court can do, and it is why Peter can ask this of people with no other recourse.

verseByVerse.quote: He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. By his wounds you have been healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree.' And here Peter steps decisively past example. Christ has been the pattern for four verses; now he does something no follower can imitate.

The verb 'bore' is the one used in the Greek Old Testament for carrying a sacrifice up to the altar. And 'the tree' is not a poetic word for cross — it is the term from Deuteronomy 21:23: cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree. Peter used the same phrase preaching in Acts (5:30; 10:39), and it is his settled way of saying that Christ went under the curse.

'In his body' anchors it. Not a spiritual transaction conducted elsewhere but sins carried in a physical body, up a hill, on a specific afternoon.

Then the purpose: 'that we might die to sin and live to righteousness.' The substitution has a moral aim. He did not bear sins so that we could continue in them, and Peter has been arguing for two chapters that the atonement produces holiness rather than excusing its absence.

'By his wounds you have been healed' is Isaiah 53:5, and the word for wounds means the welt or bruise left by a lash. Peter is writing to household slaves. Many of them had such marks on their own backs, and he tells them that the marks on his are what healed them.

That is not a promise of physical healing, and reading it so misses what Isaiah and Peter both mean — the healing is from sin, as the first half of the verse makes plain. But for a beaten slave the image would have gone in like a nail: he has been where you are, and his stripes did what yours never could.

verseByVerse.quote: For you were straying like sheep, but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'For you were straying like sheep.' Isaiah 53:6 again, and Peter keeps the prophet's picture: all we like sheep have gone astray, each turning to his own way.

The imperfect tense describes a settled condition rather than an incident. Straying was what they were doing, continuously — and sheep do not run away deliberately. They drift, head down, one mouthful at a time, until they look up and the flock is gone.

'But have now returned.' The verb can be read as passive — you were turned back — which fits everything Peter has said about being caused to be born again (1:3) and called out of darkness (2:9). Sheep are not famous for finding their own way home.

'To the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls.' Two titles, and both are chosen with care for these readers.

Shepherd is the tender one, and it carries Psalm 23 and Ezekiel 34 and John 10 with it. Overseer is episkopos — the guardian, the one who watches over; the same word translated 'bishop' when it names a church officer. Peter gives the title first to Christ, and he will call himself merely a fellow elder in chapter 5.

And of everyone in the New Testament, Peter had the most reason to write this sentence. He had strayed himself, spectacularly and in public, and he had been turned back — by a look across a courtyard and a charcoal fire on a beach where he was asked three times whether he loved him and then told to feed the sheep.

So the chapter that began with newborn infants craving milk ends with a shepherd who goes after strays. Both images are about being kept alive by someone else's care, which is the only thing Peter has offered these people from the start.
