3.title: Suffering for Righteousness: Wives, Husbands, and Christ's Victory
3.overview: Chapter 3 completes the household code (wives and husbands, vv. 1–7), calls the whole community to the posture of suffering love (vv. 8–17), and then grounds everything in the most theologically dense paragraph of the letter (vv. 18–22): Christ's death, his proclamation to the imprisoned spirits, his resurrection, and his ascension to the right hand of God with all authorities subject to him. The movement is from the household to the cosmos: Christ's victory over every power is the ultimate ground of the believer's endurance in any form of unjust suffering.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Likewise wives are to be subject to their own husbands, so that husbands who do not obey the word may be won without a word by their wives' conduct (v.1), seeing their respectful and pure behaviour (v.2). Their adorning is not to be the external braiding of hair, gold and clothing (v.3), but the hidden person of the heart, with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, very precious in God's sight (v.4). So the holy women who hoped in God used to adorn themselves (v.5), as Sarah obeyed Abraham and called him lord — and they are her children if they do good and fear nothing that is frightening (v.6).

Likewise husbands are to live with their wives in an understanding way, honouring the woman as the weaker vessel, since she is a fellow heir of the grace of life — so that their prayers may not be hindered (v.7).
verseByVerse.theology:
Reading This Passage Rightly

'Likewise' ties the paragraph to 2:23, where Christ did not revile in return but kept entrusting himself to the just Judge. What follows applies that pattern — to slaves, to wives, and in verse 7 to husbands. Nobody in the household is exempt from it.

The situation is specific and should not be generalised past what Peter says. He addresses women married to men who 'do not obey the word'. In that world a wife took her husband's religion, so a woman converted alone had done something socially outrageous and had no legal recourse and no way out. The stated purpose is evangelistic — that he may be won — and 'without a word' is realistic: she has probably already said it.

It must be said plainly that this is not a text about tolerating abuse. Peter describes witness within a marriage, not endurance of violence; the same paragraph tells a husband his prayers will be blocked if he mistreats his wife, and Scripture everywhere sets God against those who oppress the vulnerable. Anyone using verse 1 to keep a woman in danger is using it against its own author.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The three items in verse 3 were the recognised display of a wealthy Roman woman — elaborate braiding took hours and a slave to do it. Peter is not forbidding clothes, or the sentence would forbid the third item absolutely; he is speaking of where a woman's adorning is located. And note he does not tell her to stop adorning herself. He tells her to move the adornment, to the one place where it will not perish — the fourth time in this letter he has set something against everything that decays.

Now: 'Gentle and quiet' needs rescuing from a caricature. Praus is strength under control, the word used of a broken horse and the word the Lord uses of himself; quiet means settled, not agitated. Neither means timid, silent or without opinions — and the paragraph ends in courage: 'do not fear anything that is frightening.' Her composure is not fragility. Note too what Peter does with 'weaker vessel': both are vessels, the comparison is almost certainly physical strength, and the weakness is given as the reason for honour rather than for command — which inverts the ordinary logic of power completely.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, wives, be subject to your own husbands, so that even if some do not obey the word, they may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives, when they see your respectful and pure conduct.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Likewise' ties this to what precedes, and that matters for reading it rightly. Peter has just described Christ, who did not revile in return and kept entrusting himself to the just Judge (2:23). What follows is that pattern applied — first to slaves, now to wives, and in verse 7 to husbands. Nobody in the household is exempt.

The situation is specific and it should not be generalised past what Peter says. He is addressing women married to men who 'do not obey the word' — unbelieving husbands. In that world a wife was expected to take her husband's religion; a woman who had become a Christian alone had done something socially outrageous and was in a genuinely precarious position, with no legal recourse and no way out.

'Be subject to your own husbands.' The word is the military-order term Peter used of citizens and the state (2:13) and will use of the whole congregation (5:5). It is not a claim about worth — verse 7 will call her a fellow heir — and it is not obedience to men in general. It is your own husband.

Then the purpose, and it is evangelistic: 'so that they may be won without a word.' The aim is her husband's conversion. Peter is not describing a permanent arrangement of the sexes so much as giving a woman with no power a strategy that might actually save the man she is married to.

'Without a word' is the striking phrase, and it is realistic. She has probably already said it, and saying it again will not help. What is left is the thing he cannot argue with: 'when they see your respectful and pure conduct' — a life observed daily at close quarters over years.

It should be said plainly that this is not a text about tolerating abuse. Peter is describing witness within a marriage, not endurance of violence; the same letter tells husbands their prayers will be blocked if they mistreat their wives, and Scripture everywhere sets God against those who oppress the vulnerable. Anyone using verse 1 to keep a woman in danger is using it against its own author.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not let your adorning be external—the braiding of hair and the putting on of gold jewelry, or the clothing you wear— but let your adorning be the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God's sight is very precious.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Do not let your adorning be external.' Three items are named — braided hair, gold jewellery, fine clothing — and they were the recognised display of a wealthy Roman woman. Elaborate braiding took hours and a slave to do it.

Peter is not forbidding clothes, since the sentence would then forbid the third item absolutely. He is speaking of where a woman's adorning is located: what she is counting on to make her worth looking at.

'But let your adorning be the hidden person of the heart.' The contrast is outer and visible against inner and hidden — and note that Peter does not tell her to stop adorning herself. He tells her to move the adornment.

'With the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit.' That word imperishable again, for the fourth time in the letter — the inheritance (1:4), the ransom (1:18), the seed (1:23), and now this. Peter keeps setting one thing beside everything that decays, and hair and gold and cloth all belong to the perishing side.

'Gentle and quiet' needs rescuing from a caricature. Gentle is praus — the word for strength under control, used of a broken horse, and the word the Lord uses of himself: I am gentle and lowly in heart. Quiet means settled, tranquil, not agitated. Neither word means timid, silent or without opinions.

And it is a description of exactly what such a woman most needed. A Christian wife in a hostile household, unable to argue and unable to leave, is offered composure that does not depend on her circumstances improving.

'Which in God's sight is very precious.' There is the point of the whole paragraph. She is in a house where she is not valued and a society that valued the braided hair; Peter tells her what she looks like from the one perspective that will still be there in a thousand years — and the word for precious is the one used of Christ himself in 2:4.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is how the holy women who hoped in God used to adorn themselves, by submitting to their own husbands, as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord. And you are her children, if you do good and do not fear anything that is frightening.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'For this is how the holy women who hoped in God used to adorn themselves.' Peter appeals to precedent, and note the phrase he uses of them: they hoped in God. That is the source of the composure just described. These were not naturally placid women; they were women whose expectation was fixed somewhere secure.

'As Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord.' The reference is to Genesis 18:12, where Sarah, told she will have a son at ninety, laughs to herself and refers to her husband as 'my lord' — the ordinary courteous term of that world.

Be honest that Sarah is a slightly surprising example, and the honesty helps rather than hurts. She laughed at God's promise; she gave Hagar to Abraham and then dealt harshly with her; she was not a model of quiet submission throughout. Peter is not holding up a flawless woman but pointing to one whose hope was in God despite everything, which is precisely the encouragement a struggling wife needs.

'And you are her children.' The same move Peter has made all through the letter: Gentile believers are given Israel's ancestry. Paul calls Christians Abraham's offspring; Peter tells Christian women they are Sarah's daughters.

Then the condition, and the second half of it is the surprise: 'if you do good and do not fear anything that is frightening.'

That is not what we expect after a paragraph on gentleness and quietness. Peter's picture of a godly wife ends in courage. The Greek echoes Proverbs 3:25, and the point is that her composure is not fragility — she is not gentle because she is afraid. A woman who has hoped in God can be quiet in a hostile house precisely because there is nothing left in it that frightens her.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, husbands, live with your wives in an understanding way, showing honor to the woman as the weaker vessel, since they are heirs with you of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Likewise, husbands.' The same word that opened the paragraph to wives, and it puts the man under the same Christ-pattern. In a culture where a husband's authority was essentially unquestioned, the mere existence of a command to him is remarkable — and Peter gives him one verse to their six, which is not a measure of importance but of who most needed the encouragement.

'Live with your wives in an understanding way' is literally according to knowledge. It requires him to know her — to have studied this particular woman well enough to live with her intelligently. That is a lifetime's work and it cannot be done at a distance, which rules out the husband who is present in the house and absent from the marriage.

'Showing honour to the woman as the weaker vessel.' The phrase has been misused and needs stating carefully. Vessel is used of both of them — she is the weaker of two vessels, so he is a vessel too. The comparison is almost certainly physical strength, which in a world without law protecting wives was the fact that mattered.

And see what Peter does with it. The weakness is given as the reason for honour, not for contempt or command. Precisely because she is more vulnerable to him, he owes her more deference. That inverts the ordinary logic of power completely.

'Since they are heirs with you of the grace of life.' Fellow heirs — equal standing, equal inheritance, the same imperishable estate of 1:4. Whatever verse 1 means, it cannot mean she is worth less, and Peter has settled that inside the same paragraph.

'So that your prayers may not be hindered.' One of the most sobering sentences in the New Testament. The verb means cut off or blocked, as a road is blocked. A man who treats his wife badly will find his prayer life obstructed — God takes her side against him, and will not carry on ordinary dealings with a man who is mistreating a fellow heir.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Finally, all are to have unity of mind, sympathy, brotherly love, a tender heart and a humble mind (v.8), repaying neither evil for evil nor reviling for reviling but blessing instead, since they were called to inherit a blessing (v.9). Peter then quotes Psalm 34: whoever would love life must keep his tongue from evil (v.10), turn from evil and do good, seek peace and pursue it (v.11), for the Lord's eyes are on the righteous and his ears open to their prayer, but his face is against evildoers (v.12).

Who will harm you if you are zealous for good (v.13)? Yet even if you suffer for righteousness you are blessed — do not fear them or be troubled (v.14), but honour Christ the Lord as holy in your hearts, always ready to make a defence to anyone who asks the reason for your hope, with gentleness and respect (v.15), keeping a good conscience so that those who revile your conduct are put to shame (v.16). It is better to suffer for doing good, if that is God's will, than for doing evil (v.17).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Forgotten Half of Verse 15

The verse is quoted constantly for its first half and the manner clause is routinely dropped: 'yet do it with gentleness and respect.' Prautes is the same word used of the wife in verse 4 — strength under control — and 'respect' is literally fear, most likely reverence toward God, which certainly rules out contempt for the questioner. An answer given harshly has not obeyed this verse, however correct its content.

Note also the situation Peter assumes. They are not going out to argue; they are being asked. Somebody has noticed something and enquired, which means the hope must have been visible enough to prompt a question — a Christian whose life raises no questions will not need this verse. And what they explain is not the atonement in the abstract but 'the hope that is in you': why you are like this, under these conditions.

Then verse 17 is the most carefully worded sentence in the paragraph. The comparison assumes suffering either way and merely asks which kind — bleak, and honest. And 'if that should be God's will' refuses to call unjust suffering an accident or the devil's victory. It falls inside the will of God, which is either intolerable or the only thing that makes it bearable.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The psalm quoted is not chosen at random. Psalm 34 was written by David after he escaped Abimelech by feigning madness — a man in real danger with no power, getting out alive — and Peter has already drawn on it at 2:3. Its first counsel to such a man concerns the mouth, which is precisely the retaliation available to the powerless and therefore the one they would actually use. 'Do not fear them, nor be troubled' comes from Isaiah 8:12, spoken to a Judah terrified of a coalition.

Now: Verses 13 and 14 look contradictory and are not — they distinguish two kinds of harm. Ordinarily a life of conspicuous good disarms hostility, but Peter is a realist and knows what happened to his Lord. So they can hurt you and cannot harm you: the worst they can do lands on a man who is thereby called blessed, which means the injury does not reach the part of him that matters. And the defeat of slander in verse 16 is by exposure rather than rebuttal — a sufficiently clean life eventually embarrasses the people describing it falsely.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, all of you, have unity of mind, sympathy, brotherly love, a tender heart, and a humble mind. Do not repay evil for evil or reviling for reviling, but on the contrary, bless, for to this you were called, that you may obtain a blessing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Finally, all of you' — the household instructions end and the whole congregation is addressed. Five qualities follow, and they are all relational.

'Unity of mind' is like-mindedness, thinking together — not uniformity of opinion but a shared outlook. 'Sympathy' is literally suffering-with, and it is the root of our word: feeling what the other feels. In a persecuted network of congregations that was not sentiment but survival.

'Brotherly love' is philadelphia, family affection, and Peter has used it before (1:22). 'A tender heart' translates the gut-word — the visceral term for compassion. And 'a humble mind' is the word Christianity effectively invented as a virtue, since in classical Greek the root was mostly an insult.

Then the command that everything has been building toward: 'Do not repay evil for evil or reviling for reviling.' Note the second half. It is not only violence that is forbidden but the returned insult — which is the retaliation actually available to people with no power, and therefore the one they would actually use.

'But on the contrary, bless.' Not merely refrain. The instruction is not neutrality but active good — speaking well of, and asking God's favour on, the people slandering you. It is the Lord's own command (Luke 6:28), and Peter had heard it.

'For to this you were called, that you may obtain a blessing.' The called-to language again from 2:21. And the last clause is not a bargain — bless in order to be paid — but a description of the economy they are now in. They were called to inherit blessing, and blessing is therefore what they have to give away. You hand on what you were given.

verseByVerse.quote: For "Whoever desires to love life and see good days, let him keep his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit; let him turn away from evil and do good; let him seek peace and pursue it. For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter supports the command with Psalm 34:12-16, and the choice is not accidental. He has already quoted this psalm in 2:3, and it is the psalm David wrote after escaping Abimelech by pretending to be insane — a man in real danger, with no power, getting out alive. It is the right psalm for these readers.

'Whoever desires to love life and see good days.' The offer is put as an invitation to ordinary human longing. Peter is not sneering at the wish for a good life; he is telling them where it is found.

And the first instruction is about the mouth: 'let him keep his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit.' Which is exactly the point at issue. He has just forbidden reviling in return, and the psalm's first counsel to a man in danger is the same — control what you say when they come at you.

'Let him turn away from evil and do good.' Both halves, and in that order. Avoidance and then action, which is the pattern the New Testament keeps: put off, and put on.

'Let him seek peace and pursue it.' The second verb is the hunting word — chase it down. Peace here is not passivity; it is something you go after, and it will not be found by waiting for it to arrive.

Then the ground, and it is the reason any of this is possible: 'For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer.' Two organs of attention. He is watching, and he is listening — which is precisely what a slandered congregation could not be sure of.

'But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.' Peter includes the hard half, and it belongs. The reason a Christian can decline to return the insult is not that the insult does not matter. It is that it has been noticed by someone better placed to deal with it — the same argument as 2:23, where Christ handed the case to the one who judges justly.

verseByVerse.quote: Now who is there to harm you if you are zealous for what is good? But even if you should suffer for righteousness' sake, you will be blessed. Have no fear of them, nor be troubled,
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now who is there to harm you if you are zealous for what is good?' The question expects the answer nobody — and then verse 14 immediately concedes that somebody might.

That is not a contradiction; it is a distinction between two kinds of harm. Ordinarily, a life of conspicuous good does disarm hostility, and Peter has already made that his strategy (2:12, 15). But he is a realist, and he knows what happened to his Lord.

'But even if you should suffer for righteousness' sake, you will be blessed.' The construction in Greek suggests a possibility rather than a certainty — it may happen. And 'blessed' is the Beatitude word: Peter is quoting his Lord almost directly (Matt 5:10), and he had been on the hillside when it was said.

So the answer to 'who can harm you?' is that they can hurt you and cannot harm you. The worst they can do lands on a man who is thereby called blessed, which means the injury does not reach the part of him that matters.

'Have no fear of them, nor be troubled.' The words are from Isaiah 8:12, and the context there is worth knowing: Judah was terrified of an alliance forming against it, and Isaiah told them not to fear what the people feared, but to honour the LORD of hosts as holy — which is the next verse Peter quotes.

Two commands, and they are different. Do not fear them deals with the object; do not be troubled deals with the inner state, the agitation that persists after the threat has passed. Peter addresses both, and neither is a demand to feel nothing. Isaiah's word to a frightened nation was not that the danger was imaginary.

verseByVerse.quote: but in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect,
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But in your hearts honour Christ the Lord as holy.' This is the positive replacement for the fear just forbidden, and the logic is displacement: one fear drives out another. Isaiah told Judah to fear the LORD of hosts instead of the coalition, and Peter does the same — with one change he clearly intends. Isaiah's 'the LORD of hosts' becomes 'Christ the Lord'.

'Always being prepared to make a defence to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you.' The word for defence is apologia, the speech for the defence in a courtroom — and for these readers that was not always metaphorical.

Note the shape of the situation Peter assumes. They are not going out to argue; they are being asked. Somebody has noticed something and enquired. Which means the 'hope that is in you' must have been visible enough to prompt a question — and a Christian whose life raises no questions will not need this verse.

And observe what they are asked to explain. Not the doctrine of the atonement in general, but the hope in you — why you are like this, under these conditions. It is personal testimony grounded in reasons, which is why 'always being prepared' means having thought about it in advance.

Then the manner, and it is half the verse though it is usually the forgotten half: 'yet do it with gentleness and respect.'

Gentleness is prautes, the same word used of the wife in verse 4 — strength under control. Respect is literally fear, most likely reverence toward God, though it certainly rules out contempt for the questioner. Either way the point stands: an answer given harshly has not obeyed this verse, however correct its content. Peter is describing a man who honours Christ in his heart, and it comes out as courtesy to the person interrogating him.

verseByVerse.quote: having a good conscience, so that, when you are slandered, those who revile your good behavior in Christ may be put to shame. For it is better to suffer for doing good, if that should be God's will, than for doing evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Having a good conscience.' The defence of verse 15 requires a life to stand on. A man with something to hide cannot give a straight answer about his hope, because he knows the follow-up question.

'So that, when you are slandered, those who revile your good behaviour in Christ may be put to shame.' Note again that Peter says when. He has assumed the slander throughout the letter, and here he describes precisely how it is defeated.

The mechanism is exposure. The accusation is made publicly; the life is then observed publicly; and the gap between them shames the accuser. Peter is not promising the slander will stop, and he is not recommending a rebuttal. He is saying that a sufficiently clean life eventually embarrasses the people describing it falsely.

And there is a sharp phrase inside it: they revile 'your good behaviour in Christ.' What is actually being attacked is not the Christians but Christ in them, which is why the conduct matters so much and why the vindication is finally his.

Then verse 17, which is the most carefully worded sentence in the paragraph: 'For it is better to suffer for doing good, if that should be God's will, than for doing evil.'

Two things in it. First, the comparison assumes suffering either way and simply asks which kind. That is bleak and it is honest — Peter never suggests the alternative to suffering for righteousness is no suffering at all.

Second, and most important: 'if that should be God's will.' Peter will not let unjust suffering be described as an accident, an oversight, or the devil's victory. It falls inside the will of God — which is either intolerable or the only thing that makes it bearable, and this letter has been arguing for the second since chapter 1.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — Christ's Suffering and Cosmic Victory
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Christ suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring us to God — put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit (v.18), in which he went and proclaimed to the spirits in prison (v.19), who formerly did not obey while God's patience waited in the days of Noah, when eight persons were brought safely through water (v.20). Baptism corresponds to this and now saves — not as removal of dirt from the body but as an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ (v.21), who has gone into heaven and is at God's right hand, with angels, authorities and powers subjected to him (v.22).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirits in Prison: What Can and Cannot Be Said

These are among the most disputed verses in the New Testament, and honesty serves better than confidence. Three readings have serious support. The first takes it of Christ preaching through Noah by his pre-incarnate Spirit to that generation, now 'spirits in prison' because dead and under judgement — which fits the immediate mention of Noah. The second takes 'spirits' in its more usual New Testament sense of angelic beings, the fallen powers held in confinement (2 Pet 2:4; Jude 6), to whom the risen Christ announced his triumph on his way to the Father's right hand; the word for 'proclaimed' is the herald's word rather than the word for preaching the gospel, and verse 22 does end with angels and authorities subjected. The third, older view has Christ descending between death and resurrection; it has ancient support but the text does not clearly say it.

The second has most in its favour on the wording, the first on the context. What no reading may do is make this a promise of a second opportunity after death — the announcement is a proclamation of triumph, not an offer, and Scripture elsewhere excludes it (Heb 9:27).

Verse 21 needs the same care and largely settles itself. Peter says baptism 'now saves you' and then immediately rules out the mechanical reading — 'not as a removal of dirt from the body' — and grounds the saving in 'the resurrection of Jesus Christ'. Baptism saves the way a wedding ring marries you: it is the sign and pledge of a union whose power lies entirely elsewhere.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The pastoral point of the Noah reference survives every reading of verse 19, which is presumably why Peter included it. Noah was a tiny minority — 'a few, that is, eight persons' — in a world entirely against him, and God's patience waited while he built. That is exactly the situation of the people receiving this letter, and the eight were not lost.

Now: Verse 18 states the purpose of the cross as access: 'that he might bring us to God', a verb used of leading someone into a king's presence and, in the Greek Old Testament, of presenting priests for consecration. The end is not an improved life or even an escaped hell but God himself; everything else is arrangements for getting there. And verse 22 is the letter's whole answer to intimidation — every power these readers feared is named and placed, subjected, past tense, already done. The man they follow was rejected by men, suffered unjustly, and is now seated with the authorities under his feet. That is the sequence Peter has been asking them to trust for their own lives since the first verse.

verseByVerse.quote: For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
'For Christ also suffered once for sins.' The 'for' connects it to verse 17: if unjust suffering can be God's will, here is the supreme case of it.

'Once' — hapax, once for all, never to be repeated. It is the word Hebrews builds its argument on, and it rules out any notion of a sacrifice that must be topped up.

'The righteous for the unrighteous.' Four words, and they are as compact a statement of substitution as the New Testament contains. Singular and plural: one righteous man in the place of many unrighteous ones. And note the exchange is not a transaction between equals — it is the innocent standing where the guilty were.

'That he might bring us to God.' The verb is used of leading someone into the presence of a king, and in the Greek Old Testament of bringing a sacrifice to the altar and of presenting priests for consecration. The purpose of the cross is stated as access — not primarily to make us safe or happy but to bring us into a presence we had no business entering.

Sit with that with, because it names what salvation is finally for. The end is not an improved life or even an escaped hell. It is God himself, and everything else is arrangements for getting there.

'Being put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit.' The two datives are parallel and describe two spheres: killed as far as bodily human life goes, made alive in the realm of the Spirit. Most likely a reference to the resurrection state rather than to his soul surviving — and it sets up the notoriously difficult verse that follows.

verseByVerse.quote: in which he went and proclaimed to the spirits in prison, because they formerly did not obey, when God's patience waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was being prepared, in which a few, that is, eight persons, were brought safely through water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are among the most disputed verses in the New Testament, and honesty about that serves better than confidence. Godly readers have differed for centuries, and the passage should be handled with the humility it demands.

'In which he went and proclaimed to the spirits in prison.' The three main readings are worth knowing.

The first takes it of Christ preaching through Noah, by his pre-incarnate Spirit, to the people of Noah's generation — who are now 'spirits in prison' because they are dead and under judgement. This fits the reference to Noah's preaching and avoids a second chance after death, which Scripture elsewhere rules out (Heb 9:27).

The second takes 'spirits' in its more usual New Testament sense of angelic beings — the fallen angels associated with Genesis 6, held in confinement (2 Pet 2:4; Jude 6). On this reading the risen Christ, on his way to the Father's right hand (v.22), announced his triumph to the imprisoned powers. The word for proclaimed is the herald's word, not the word for preaching the gospel, and verse 22 does end with angels and authorities subjected to him.

The third, older view is that Christ descended between his death and resurrection to proclaim victory or release. It has ancient support but the text does not clearly say it.

The second reading has the most in its favour on the wording, and the first has the most on the immediate mention of Noah. What no reading may do is turn this into a promise of a second opportunity after death, since the announcement is a proclamation of triumph rather than an offer.

And the pastoral point survives every reading, which is presumably why Peter included it. Noah was a tiny minority — 'a few, that is, eight persons' — in a world entirely against him, and God's patience waited while he built. That is the situation of the people receiving this letter, and the eight were not lost.

verseByVerse.quote: Baptism, which corresponds to this, now saves you, not as a removal of dirt from the body but as an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who has gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God, with angels, authorities, and powers having been subjected to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Baptism, which corresponds to this, now saves you.' Another sentence that needs careful reading rather than either alarm or overstatement.

The word for corresponds means antitype — the thing the earlier pattern pointed to. The flood pattern is: judgement falls, water is the instrument, and a few are brought safely through it into a new world.

Peter says baptism 'now saves you' — and then immediately explains what he does and does not mean, which settles the matter. 'Not as a removal of dirt from the body.' The water itself does nothing; he rules out the mechanical reading in the same breath he raises it.

'But as an appeal to God for a good conscience.' The word can mean an appeal or a pledge — either the cry of a man asking God to give him a clear conscience, or the answer of a good conscience given to God. Either way it locates the saving power in what is happening between the person and God, not in the liquid.

'Through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.' And there is the final safeguard. Baptism saves the way a wedding ring marries you — it is the sign and pledge of a union whose power lies entirely elsewhere. What saves is the resurrection; baptism is how a person is joined to it and says so publicly.

Then verse 22, and the letter's whole answer to intimidation: 'who has gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God, with angels, authorities, and powers having been subjected to him.'

Every power these readers were afraid of — the magistrate, the mob, the emperor, and whatever stood behind them — is named and placed. Subjected, past tense, already done. The man they follow was rejected by men (2:4), suffered unjustly (2:23), and is now seated with the authorities under his feet; and that is the sequence Peter has been asking them to trust for their own lives since the first verse.

4.title: Stewards of Grace: The Meaning of Suffering
4.overview: Chapter 4 returns to the theme of suffering but with a new theological frame: the end of all things is at hand (v. 7), so suffering must be understood eschatologically. The first half (vv. 1–11) grounds the break with the old life and the obligations of the new community in the nearness of the end. The second half (vv. 12–19) addresses the 'fiery trial' directly: do not be surprised by it; it is the expected furnace-testing of the gospel age; rejoice to share Christ's sufferings; and commit yourselves to the faithful Creator. The chapter is the letter's most direct pastoral address to a suffering community.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Stewards of God's Varied Grace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Since Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same way of thinking, for whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin (v.1), so as to live the rest of the time for the will of God rather than human passions (v.2). The past time is enough for sensuality, drunkenness and lawless idolatry (v.3); the neighbours are astonished that you no longer join the flood, and malign you (v.4) — but they will answer to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead (v.5). This is why the gospel was preached even to those who are now dead: though judged in the flesh as people are, they might live in the spirit as God does (v.6).

The end of all things is at hand, so be self-controlled and sober-minded for the sake of your prayers (v.7). Above all, keep loving one another earnestly, since love covers a multitude of sins (v.8). Show hospitality without grumbling (v.9). As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another as good stewards of God's varied grace (v.10) — whoever speaks, as one speaking oracles of God; whoever serves, by the strength God supplies — so that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ (v.11).
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Difficult Verses, Handled Plainly

Verse 1's 'whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin' cannot mean suffering makes a person sinless — that contradicts every command which follows. It may refer to Christ himself, done with sin having dealt with it once for all (3:18); more likely, given the 'whoever', it describes what suffering does to a believer's relationship with sin. Verse 2 supplies the sense: the result is a life directed to God's will rather than human passions. It is about direction, not perfection — a man who has paid a real price for Christ has already found out what the alternative was worth, and has stopped negotiating.

Verse 6's 'the gospel was preached even to those who are dead' most likely means Christians who have since died — a live pastoral problem, since believers were dying and the obvious taunt was that their faith had done them no good. The verse answers exactly that: they were judged in the flesh as everyone is, and it was not the last word. The reading that offers a second chance after death cannot stand — it contradicts Hebrews 9:27 and empties the New Testament's own urgency — and it is not needed, since the natural reading is both simpler and more comforting.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The six vices of verse 3 are all social, and much of it was religious — the temple feasts of a Greek city ran on precisely this. That is why leaving cost these people their friends, and why the neighbours' reaction in verse 4 is bewilderment rather than principled objection. When everyone is being carried by a current, the person standing still is an implied criticism of everyone moving past him. The slander this letter addresses begins there, in social withdrawal, not in theological disagreement.

Now: Note what Peter draws from 'the end of all things is at hand'. You might expect a call to dramatic action; he says be clear-headed, and pray. And the purpose is the surprising part — the sober mind is 'for the sake of your prayers', because an agitated or intoxicated mind cannot pray. Most people's prayer life fails through mental clutter rather than unbelief. And 'love covers a multitude of sins' is not concealment of wrongdoing but the refusal to circulate it: a dozen households meeting weekly in someone's front room will generate friction constantly, and whether small offences get covered or passed on decides whether such a church survives.

verseByVerse.quote: Since therefore Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same way of thinking, for whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin, so as to live for the rest of the time in the flesh no longer for human passions but for the will of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Arm yourselves with the same way of thinking.' The verb is a soldier's word — take up your weapons — and what Peter hands them is not a shield but a thought. The armament is mental: the settled conviction that suffering is the road Christ took.

That is a realistic piece of pastoral care. A Christian ambushed by suffering he did not expect is far more likely to collapse than one who decided in advance what it means. Peter is telling them to make the decision before the trial rather than during it.

Then the difficult clause: 'whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin.' Read flatly it seems to say that suffering makes a person sinless, which is plainly untrue and contradicts the commands that follow.

Two readings carry weight. It may refer to Christ himself — he suffered and is now done with sin, having dealt with it once for all (3:18). Or, more likely given the 'whoever', it describes what suffering does to a believer's relationship with sin. The man who has genuinely paid a price for following Christ has made a decisive break: he has already chosen, under pressure, and the choosing settles something.

Verse 2 supports the second reading by stating the result: 'so as to live for the rest of the time in the flesh no longer for human passions but for the will of God.' The break is about direction, not perfection. Something has been finished with.

Anyone who has suffered for a conviction knows the effect. Once you have lost something real for Christ, the appeal of what you gave up is permanently reduced — you have already found out what it was worth. That is not sinlessness. It is a man who has stopped negotiating.

verseByVerse.quote: For the time that is past suffices for doing what the Gentiles want to do, living in sensuality, passions, drunkenness, orgies, drinking parties, and lawless idolatry. With respect to this they are surprised when you do not join them in the same flood of debauchery, and they malign you;
verseByVerse.commentary:
'For the time that is past suffices.' The understatement is almost dry — you have given that quite enough of your life already. Peter does not argue them out of their old habits; he simply says the account is closed.

Then six words for what they had left, and the list is unsparing: sensuality, passions, drunkenness, orgies, drinking parties, and lawless idolatry. These were not abstractions. Much of it was religious — the temple feasts of a Greek city ran on exactly this, and the last item names what held the rest together.

Note that the whole list is social. Every item is something done in company, which is precisely why leaving it cost these people their friends.

'With respect to this they are surprised when you do not join them.' The verb means to be taken aback, thrown by something unaccountable. Their neighbours are genuinely puzzled — not offended on principle but bewildered that anyone would opt out.

'The same flood of debauchery' is a vivid word: an outpouring, a torrent, something running out of its channel. And the picture explains the reaction. When everyone is being carried along by a current, the person standing still is not merely different — he is an implied criticism of everyone moving past him.

'And they malign you.' That is the mechanism of the slander this whole letter addresses. It does not begin in theological objection. It begins in social withdrawal: you stopped coming, and the people you stopped coming to have drawn their own conclusions about why.

verseByVerse.quote: but they will give account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead. For this is why the gospel was preached even to those who are dead, that though judged in the flesh the way people are, they might live in the spirit the way God does.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But they will give account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead.' The answer to being maligned is not vindication now but a court later — the same move as 2:23, where Christ entrusted himself to the one who judges justly.

'Ready' is the sharp word. Not eventually, not one day. He is standing by, prepared, and the delay is patience rather than absence.

Then verse 6, another genuinely disputed sentence: 'this is why the gospel was preached even to those who are dead.'

The most likely reading, and the one that fits the argument, is that these are Christians who have since died — people who heard the gospel while alive and are now dead. That was a live pastoral problem: believers had been dying, sometimes under persecution, and the obvious taunt from neighbours was that their faith had done them no good at all.

The verse answers exactly that. 'Though judged in the flesh the way people are' — they died, which is the judgement all flesh comes under — 'they might live in the spirit the way God does.' The verdict of death was passed on them as it is on everyone. It was not the last word.

The alternative reading, that the gospel is preached to the already-dead offering a second chance, cannot stand: it contradicts Hebrews 9:27 and empties the urgency of the New Testament's own preaching. And it is not needed, because the natural reading is both simpler and more comforting.

So the pastoral force is this. A congregation burying its members under slander is told that death is the judgement everybody receives in the flesh, and that it settles nothing about the verdict that matters.

verseByVerse.quote: The end of all things is at hand; therefore be self-controlled and sober-minded for the sake of your prayers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The end of all things is at hand.' The word for end is telos — not merely the stopping but the goal, the point everything has been heading for. Peter is not announcing that things will run out; he is saying they will arrive.

And 'at hand' has drawn a great deal of comment, since two thousand years have passed. The New Testament's consistent posture is not a calculated date but a nearness that makes everything urgent. Peter himself writes that with the Lord a day is as a thousand years (2 Pet 3:8), so he was not making a prediction he could be caught out by.

What matters is what he draws from it, and it is startling. Given that the end is near, you might expect a call to dramatic action — evangelise harder, wind up your affairs, gather on a hillside. Peter says: be self-controlled and sober-minded, and pray.

Both words have appeared already. Sober-minded is from 1:13 — clear-headed, unintoxicated, seeing things as they are. Self-controlled is its companion. Peter's answer to eschatological urgency is a steady head.

'For the sake of your prayers.' And there is the purpose, which is the surprising part. The clear head is not for its own sake or for better decisions. It is so that they can pray — because a mind that is agitated, frightened or intoxicated cannot.

That is worth taking personally. Most people's prayer life fails not through unbelief but through mental clutter, and Peter treats the clearing of the head as a discipline undertaken specifically so that prayer becomes possible again.

verseByVerse.quote: Above all, keep loving one another earnestly, since love covers a multitude of sins. Show hospitality to one another without grumbling.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Above all, keep loving one another earnestly.' The priority is stated plainly, and 'earnestly' is the stretched-out word from 1:22 — love at full extension, the effort of a muscle under strain.

'Since love covers a multitude of sins.' The phrase comes from Proverbs 10:12: hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all offences. And 'covers' must be read rightly. This is not concealment of wrongdoing, and it is not the covering that atones — only Christ's blood does that.

It means love does not spread things. It refuses to publish, to relitigate, to keep the account open. A congregation of a dozen households under persecution, meeting weekly in someone's front room, will generate friction constantly; and the difference between a church that survives that and one that tears itself apart is whether small offences get covered or circulated.

Then verse 9, and it follows for a very practical reason: 'Show hospitality to one another without grumbling.'

Hospitality was not optional in that world. There were no church buildings — the congregation met in a home, and somebody's floor took the wear. Travelling Christians needed lodging, since inns were expensive and often disreputable. Peter's word means love-of-strangers, and it was a costly practical burden borne by whoever had the largest room.

Which is exactly why 'without grumbling' is attached. Peter knows that the household hosting the church is the household most likely to resent it, and that the resentment will come out as muttering rather than refusal. The command is not to open your door — they were already doing that. It is to stop complaining about the cost of it.

verseByVerse.quote: As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of God's varied grace: whoever speaks, as one who speaks oracles of God; whoever serves, as one who serves by the strength that God supplies—in order that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ. To him belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'As each has received a gift.' Each — the word carries the weight. Peter assumes that every member of these scattered congregations has been given something, and there is no category of Christian who has not.

'Use it to serve one another.' The gift is not for the possessor. It arrives already assigned, and the direction is toward other people — which settles the question of what gifts are for before anyone can make them a measure of standing.

'As good stewards of God's varied grace.' A steward manages what belongs to somebody else, and will be asked about it. And varied is a lovely word — literally many-coloured, used of an embroidered cloth. God's grace is not issued in one shade; the congregation is a fabric of different colours, and a single-coloured church has lost something God intended to be seen.

Then Peter divides all gifts into two: 'whoever speaks' and 'whoever serves'. Word and deed, and both are needed.

'As one who speaks oracles of God.' That is a weighty standard. Not that every Christian's words are inspired, but that anyone speaking in the congregation should handle the responsibility as though delivering God's own utterances — carefully, and not casually.

'As one who serves by the strength that God supplies.' The verb is the choregos word again — the wealthy citizen who funded a chorus and paid for everything it needed. The servant does not run on his own reserves.

And the purpose gathers both: 'in order that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ.' Which is why Peter breaks into doxology mid-letter. A man thinking about gifts rightly ends up talking about God rather than about gifts.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Do not be surprised at the fiery trial that comes to test you, as though something strange were happening (v.12), but rejoice insofar as you share Christ's sufferings, so that you may be glad when his glory is revealed (v.13). If you are insulted for the name of Christ you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you (v.14).

Let none of you suffer as a murderer, thief, evildoer or meddler (v.15); but if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed but glorify God in that name (v.16). For it is time for judgement to begin at the household of God — and if with us, what of those who do not obey the gospel (v.17)? If the righteous is scarcely saved, what will become of the ungodly (v.18)? Therefore let those who suffer according to God's will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good (v.19).
verseByVerse.theology:
Judgement Beginning at Home

Verse 17 reframes everything the letter has described, and the idea is Ezekiel's: when judgement fell on Jerusalem the command was to begin at the sanctuary (Ezek 9:6). So the suffering these congregations endure is not merely hostility from outside but the first movement of God's own sifting — which is not a comfortable thought and is a clarifying one. Their trials are not outside God's programme and are not evidence of his absence. He has started, and he has started at home.

The argument then runs from lesser to greater and Peter leaves it as a question, which is more forceful than a statement — the reader does the arithmetic about his own persecutors, and that is more sobering than being told. And 'scarcely saved' in verse 18 does not mean saved by a narrow margin or with barely enough grace; it means saved with difficulty, through the fire this letter has been describing. Salvation is certain and the road is hard, and Peter never pretends otherwise.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: 'Christian' occurs only three times in the New Testament, and this is the only place a believer uses it of himself. It was coined at Antioch (Acts 11:26) and was almost certainly an outsiders' nickname — Christ-people. So Peter takes the label the neighbours were using as an insult and tells them to wear it: that is what not being ashamed means here, and the mockers who supplied the word find it converted into an occasion of praise.

Now: The fourth item in verse 15 does not belong with the first three, and the placing is deliberate. The word for 'meddler' appears nowhere else in Greek literature and Peter may have coined it; setting the busybody beside murderers and thieves is startling until you consider a small, suspected minority, where a Christian who cannot keep out of his neighbours' business generates hostility and then mistakes it for persecution. And the closing verse gives the letter's answer: entrust is the deposit word used of Christ in 2:23, and the title chosen for God — Creator, used of him nowhere else in the New Testament — means a man handing over his soul is giving it back to the one who made it. Note that this is done 'while doing good', not instead of acting.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you. But rejoice insofar as you share Christ's sufferings, that you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you.' The word for surprised is the one used in verse 4 of the pagans, who were taken aback that Christians would not join them. Peter turns it round: they are astonished at you; do not you be astonished at this.

'The fiery trial' is literally the burning — the word used of smelting metal, and it reaches back to 1:7 where faith is refined like gold. Peter has not changed his mind about what the fire is for.

'When it comes', not if. And 'to test you' names the purpose, which is the whole point of the sentence. A trial with a purpose is a different experience from a trial without one, though the heat is identical.

'As though something strange were happening to you.' There is the pastoral target. The danger is not the suffering but the interpretation — the conclusion that this is abnormal, that it means God has withdrawn, that other Christians somewhere are having an easier time and must be doing it better.

Peter's answer is that persecution is not a deviation from the Christian life but a normal feature of it. Which is a hard word and a strangely freeing one: a great deal of the pain of suffering is the suspicion that it should not be happening.

'But rejoice insofar as you share Christ's sufferings.' Note the careful measure — insofar as. Peter is not commanding joy in suffering generally, but in the specific portion of it that is genuinely a share in Christ's. And 'share' is the fellowship word: this is participation, not imitation.

'That you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed.' The joy is not two joys but one, arriving in two instalments. What is begun now under the fire will be completed at the revelation — and the second verb is the exuberant one, the word for shouting gladness.

verseByVerse.quote: If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed.' The Beatitude again, as in 3:14 — Peter keeps returning to a sermon he heard on a hillside.

Note the precision: for the name of Christ. Not for being difficult, or tactless, or socially awkward. Peter will make the distinction explicit in the very next verse, and he is careful never to let a Christian claim the blessing for trouble he brought on himself.

And insult is the specific form named. Not imprisonment or death at this stage — reviling, the ordinary daily contempt of neighbours. Which is what most Christians under pressure actually face, then and now: not a courtroom but a reputation quietly destroyed.

Then the reason, and it is one of the most remarkable statements in the letter: 'because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you.'

The verb 'rests' is the one used in Isaiah 11:2, where the Spirit of the LORD rests on the shoot from the stump of Jesse — a messianic text. Peter says the same Spirit settles on an insulted congregation in Bithynia.

And there is very likely an echo of the glory-cloud that rested on the tabernacle. The presence that filled the tent now rests on people being sworn at in the street.

Which inverts the whole appearance of things. The neighbours see a group whose reputation is in ruins. Peter says the visible shame is the outward face of an invisible glory, and that the Spirit is not merely with them despite the insults but is resting on them precisely there.

verseByVerse.quote: But let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer or as a meddler. Yet if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in that name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer.' Peter will not let the blessing of verse 14 be claimed by a Christian who has earned his trouble. The distinction has run through the letter (2:20; 3:17) and he states it once more, bluntly.

Then the fourth item, and it does not belong with the first three: 'or as a meddler.' The word appears nowhere else in Greek literature and Peter may have coined it; it means something like an overseer-of-other-people's-business.

Set beside murder and theft it is startling, and the placing is the point. Peter puts interfering in other people's affairs in a list with felonies — because in a small suspected minority, the busybody does real damage. A Christian who cannot keep out of his neighbours' business will generate hostility and then mistake it for persecution.

'Yet if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed.' The word Christian appears only three times in the New Testament, and this is the only place a believer uses it of himself. It was coined at Antioch (Acts 11:26) and was almost certainly an outsiders' nickname — Christ-people, Christ-ites.

So Peter takes the label the neighbours were using as an insult and tells them to wear it. That is what he means by not being ashamed: the name is being thrown at them, and the instruction is to catch it.

'But let him glorify God in that name.' The shame is not merely to be endured but converted. The mockers supplied the word; the Christian is to make it an occasion of praise — which takes the sting out of an insult more completely than any denial could.

verseByVerse.quote: For it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God; and if it begins with us, what will be the outcome for those who do not obey the gospel of God? And "If the righteous is scarcely saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner?" Therefore let those who suffer according to God's will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'For it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God.' A startling sentence, and it reframes everything the letter has described.

The idea is Ezekiel's. When judgement fell on Jerusalem, the command was to begin at the sanctuary (Ezek 9:6) — God's own house first. Peter is saying that the suffering these congregations are enduring is not merely persecution from outside; it is the first movement of God's own sifting, and it begins with his people.

That is not a comfortable thought and it is a clarifying one. Their trials are not outside God's programme, and they are not evidence of his absence. He has started, and he has started at home.

'And if it begins with us, what will be the outcome for those who do not obey the gospel of God?' The argument runs from lesser to greater and Peter leaves it as a question, which is more forceful than a statement. If the household is going through this, the question answers itself — and the reader is left to do the arithmetic about his persecutors, which is a far more sobering thing than being told.

Verse 18 quotes Proverbs 11:31. 'Scarcely saved' does not mean saved by a narrow margin or barely enough grace. It means saved with difficulty — through fire, through the process this letter has been describing. Salvation is certain and the road to it is hard, and Peter has never pretended otherwise.

Then the conclusion, and it is the finest sentence in the chapter: 'Therefore let those who suffer according to God's will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good.'

The verb entrust is the deposit word — the same one used of Christ in 2:23, handing his case to the just Judge. And the title chosen for God is exact: Creator, used of him nowhere else in the New Testament. A man handing over his soul is giving it back to the one who made it, and 'faithful' means the deposit will be there when he asks for it. Note also that the entrusting is done 'while doing good' — not instead of acting, but in the middle of it.
