5.title: Humble Yourselves: Elders, Community, and the God of All Grace
5.overview: The final chapter gathers the letter's ethical threads into three movements: the elders who are to shepherd (vv. 1–5), the whole community that is to humble itself under God's mighty hand and resist the devil (vv. 6–11), and the closing greetings that locate the letter in Rome and identify its bearers (vv. 12–14). The climax is one of the most beautiful benedictions in the NT: the God of all grace who called you to his eternal glory in Christ will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you (v. 10). The letter that began with scattered exiles ends with the promise that the God who scattered nothing — who chose them before the foundation of the world — will bring everything to completion.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Shepherd the Flock of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Peter exhorts the elders as a fellow elder, a witness of Christ's sufferings and a partaker in the glory to be revealed (v.1): shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight — not under compulsion but willingly, not for shameful gain but eagerly (v.2), not domineering but being examples to the flock (v.3). And when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory (v.4).

Likewise the younger are to be subject to the elders; and all of them are to tie on humility toward one another, for God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble (v.5).
verseByVerse.theology:
Three Temptations and Their Remedies

Verse 2-3 gives the most searching description of pastoral motive in Scripture, in three pairs. Not under compulsion but willingly — the danger of doing it from duty, or because nobody else will, or because you cannot see how to stop. Not for shameful gain but eagerly — money, and Peter assumes elders were paid something or the warning would be pointless. Not domineering but being examples — power, the one that ruins most; and the verb is the very word the Lord used of the rulers of the Gentiles when he said 'it shall not be so among you' (Mark 10:42-43). Peter was in the room.

Note that the alternative to domineering is not weak leadership but a costlier kind. A man who leads by command need only be obeyed; a man who leads by example has to be worth copying, which is a far harder standard to meet on a Tuesday. And archipoimen in verse 4 — chief Shepherd, a word found nowhere else in the Greek Bible — answers all three temptations at the root: nobody serves grudgingly, or for money, or by lording it, if he genuinely believes the sheep belong to someone else who is due home.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter could have written 'as an apostle' — the letter opened that way. Addressing church leaders about leading, he sets the title down and takes the same chair: sympresbyteros, fellow elder, a word found nowhere else in the New Testament and possibly coined for this sentence. And when he tells elders to shepherd the flock, the words come from the man told three times on a beach to feed the sheep, after denying he knew the Shepherd at all.

Now: The crown of verse 4 is stephanos, the victor's wreath at the games — a circle of leaves, and everyone watching knew how fast it browned. So the adjective is chosen with care: unfading, from the amaranth, the ancient symbol of what does not wither, the same root used of the inheritance in 1:4. To elders in a persecuted network of house churches — unpaid or barely paid, unnoticed outside their own street, and in danger — Peter says the recognition is coming from the only person whose opinion is final. And the verb in verse 5 means to tie on the apron a slave fastened before serving: of all men, Peter chose the image he had originally refused in the upper room (John 13:4-8).

verseByVerse.quote: So I exhort the elders among you, as a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, as well as a partaker in the glory that is going to be revealed:
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So I exhort the elders among you, as a fellow elder.' Consider what Peter does not say. He could have written 'as an apostle', and the letter opened that way (1:1). Addressing church leaders about how to lead, he sets the title down and takes the same chair they are sitting in.

Sympresbyteros — fellow elder — appears nowhere else in the New Testament. He seems to have made it for this sentence, and it is the credential he wants in play: not authority over them but experience alongside them.

'And a witness of the sufferings of Christ.' That is a claim only a handful of men could make, and it carries more than the fact of having been present. Peter had watched, from the courtyard, and had failed there. When he tells elders to shepherd the flock, the words come from the man who was told three times on a beach to feed the sheep, after denying he knew the Shepherd at all.

'As well as a partaker in the glory that is going to be revealed.' The tenses are worth noticing. He was a witness of the sufferings; he is a partaker of a glory not yet revealed. Peter puts himself and them in exactly the same position — between a suffering already seen and a glory still coming — which is where this whole letter has located its readers since the first chapter.

And there may be a memory in that word. Peter had seen glory revealed once, on the mountain, and had wanted to build shelters and stay. He writes now as a man who knows the glory is real and that it is not yet time.

verseByVerse.quote: shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight, not under compulsion, but willingly, as God would have you; not for shameful gain, but eagerly; not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight.' Two verbs, and they are the two words the New Testament uses for church leadership — shepherding and overseeing. Peter has already given both titles to Christ (2:25), which fixes the terms: these men are undershepherds, and the flock is not theirs.

'The flock of God that is among you' says it twice over. It belongs to God, and the elder is among it rather than above it.

Then three pairs, each a temptation and its remedy, and together they are the most searching description of pastoral motive in Scripture.

'Not under compulsion, but willingly.' The first danger is doing it because you have to — from duty, or because nobody else will, or because you cannot see how to stop. Peter adds 'as God would have you', which locates the willingness: not natural enthusiasm but a work taken up under God.

'Not for shameful gain, but eagerly.' Money, and Peter assumes elders were paid something or the warning would be pointless. The word for the alternative means wholeheartedly, with zeal — the opposite of a man calculating what the post returns.

'Not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock.' The third is power, and it is the one that ruins most. The verb means to lord it over — the very word the Lord used when he said the rulers of the Gentiles do this, and 'it shall not be so among you' (Mark 10:42-43). Peter was in the room.

And the alternative is not weak leadership but a costlier kind: example. A man who leads by command need only be obeyed; a man who leads by example has to be worth copying, and that is a far harder standard to meet on a Tuesday.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And when the chief Shepherd appears.' The word archipoimen occurs nowhere else in the Greek Bible, and it settles the whole passage. There is one chief Shepherd, and every elder addressed here is under him.

It also answers the three temptations of the previous verse at their root. A man who genuinely believes the flock belongs to someone else, who is coming back, will not serve grudgingly, or for money, or by domineering — because none of those makes sense if you are minding somebody else's sheep and he is due home.

'You will receive the unfading crown of glory.' The crown is stephanos, the victor's wreath at the games rather than a royal diadem — a circle of leaves, and everyone watching knew how quickly it browned.

So Peter's adjective is chosen with care: unfading, amarantinos, from the amaranth, the flower the ancients used as a symbol of what does not wither. He used the same root of the inheritance in 1:4. The wreath handed to an athlete was dead within the week; this one is made of something else.

And note what the crown is made of: 'the crown of glory' — most likely meaning the crown that consists of glory, as 'crown of life' in James 1:12 means the crown which is life. The reward is not a decoration to wear but a share in the glory Peter has just said he is a partaker of.

Which is a striking thing to promise elders in a persecuted network of house churches. Their work was unpaid or barely paid, unnoticed outside their own street, and dangerous. Peter tells them the recognition is coming from the only person whose opinion is final.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, you who are younger, be subject to the elders. Clothe yourselves, all of you, with humility toward one another, for "God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Likewise, you who are younger, be subject to the elders.' Having addressed the leaders, Peter turns to those most likely to chafe under them. The word may mean younger in years or simply those not holding office; either way the instruction is the same posture the letter has asked of citizens, slaves and wives.

Then the scope widens and takes everyone in: 'Clothe yourselves, all of you, with humility toward one another.'

The verb is unusual and vivid. It means to tie something on — it was used of the apron a slave fastened over his clothes before serving. Peter is telling the whole congregation to put on the servant's apron.

And of all the men who could have chosen that image, Peter is the one who had watched it happen. In the upper room the Lord rose from supper, laid aside his outer garments, tied a towel round himself, and washed their feet — and Peter had objected, loudly, and been told that unless he allowed it he had no part with him (John 13:4-8). The picture he reaches for here is one he originally refused.

'For God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.' The quotation is Proverbs 3:34, and James uses it too (Jas 4:6) — evidently a text the early church leaned on hard.

The word for opposes is military: to draw up in battle order against. God does not merely decline to help the proud; he takes the field opposite them. And grace, being a gift, can only be received by open hands — which is why humility is not one virtue among several here but the posture in which anything at all can be received.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–14 — Cast Your Anxieties, and Stand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Humble yourselves under God's mighty hand, so that at the proper time he may exalt you (v.6), casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you (v.7). Be sober-minded and watchful: your adversary the devil prowls like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour (v.8). Resist him, firm in faith, knowing the same sufferings are being experienced by the brotherhood throughout the world (v.9).

And after you have suffered a little while, the God of all grace, who called you to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore, confirm, strengthen and establish you (v.10). To him be the dominion forever (v.11). Peter has written briefly by Silvanus, declaring that this is the true grace of God — stand firm in it (v.12). The church at Babylon, likewise chosen, greets them, and so does Mark (v.13). Greet one another with the kiss of love; peace to all who are in Christ (v.14).
verseByVerse.theology:
Why Worry Is Treated as Pride

The grammar of verse 7 matters more than most readers notice. 'Casting all your anxieties on him' is not a separate command but a participle attached to 'humble yourselves' — the casting is how the humbling is done. We do not usually think of worry as pride, and Peter does: holding on to your anxieties is a way of insisting the situation is yours to manage, and handing them over is an act of self-lowering.

The verb is decisive — throw it, the word used of the disciples flinging their cloaks on the colt; not setting down gently, and not sharing. 'All' leaves no category too small to bother him with. And the ground is not that God is capable but that he is concerned — the word means it matters to him. To people whose neighbours had decided they were nothing, the last words of the sentence say they are on somebody's mind.

Then the four verbs of verse 10 build deliberately. Restore is the mending word — used of setting a broken bone and of repairing nets, which Peter had done for a living — and it assumes damage: the suffering will break something, and God will set it. Confirm is the word the Lord used when he told Peter that after turning again he should strengthen his brothers (Luke 22:32). And the emphatic word is himself: God will personally do the mending, which is the promise a battered congregation needed, from a man who had been broken and repaired by name.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Antidikos in verse 8 is a courtroom word — the opponent in a lawsuit, the prosecutor — which precisely describes what these readers were experiencing: public, continuous accusation. And notice what a roaring lion is doing. A lion stalking prey is silent; the roar is meant to panic the herd and drive something out of it. The noise is a weapon that works on the nerves rather than the body, and 'seeking someone' means the hunt is selective — he is looking for the one that has drifted, which is exactly what persecution does to a congregation.

Now: The encouragement in verse 9 is not relief but company: the same sufferings are being experienced by the brotherhood throughout the world. Isolation is the lion's method, and the answer is knowing you are one of many — which is why Peter wrote a circular letter to five provinces rather than a private note. And note his own summary in verse 12: after five chapters on suffering, submission and slander, he calls the whole thing grace, and their part is simply to stand in it. 'Babylon' in verse 13 is almost certainly Rome — so Peter writes to exiles from the empire's capital and calls it the place of exile, reminding them that the church at the centre of the world is as much in a foreign country as the church in Bithynia.

verseByVerse.quote: Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you, casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God.' The 'therefore' follows the proverb: since that is how God deals with pride and humility, put yourself on the right side of it.

'The mighty hand of God' is an exodus phrase — it is how the Old Testament describes God bringing Israel out of Egypt with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. And it cuts both ways, which is why it is the right image here. The hand is heavy; it is also the hand that delivers.

'So that at the proper time he may exalt you.' The lifting is his work and his timing. Peter has already used kairos, the appointed moment, of God's dealings; a man who insists on being raised now has taken the job out of the right hands.

Then verse 7, and the grammar matters more than most readers realise. 'Casting all your anxieties on him' is not a separate command. It is a participle attached to 'humble yourselves' — the casting is how the humbling is done.

That connection is easily missed and it is the heart of the verse. We do not usually think of worry as pride. Peter does: holding on to your anxieties is a way of insisting that the situation is yours to manage, and handing them over is an act of self-lowering.

'Casting' is a decisive verb — throw it, the word used of the disciples flinging their cloaks on the colt. Not setting down gently, and not sharing. And 'all' leaves no category too small to bother him with.

'Because he cares for you.' The ground of the whole thing, and it is not that he is capable but that he is concerned. The word means it matters to him. Peter is writing to people whose neighbours had decided they were nothing, and the last word of the sentence is that they are on somebody's mind.

verseByVerse.quote: Be sober-minded; be watchful. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. Resist him, firm in your faith, knowing that the same kinds of suffering are being experienced by your brotherhood throughout the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Be sober-minded; be watchful.' Two sharp imperatives, and both have appeared before (1:13; 4:7). Peter's repeated counsel to a frightened church is a clear head and open eyes.

The second word is the one from Gethsemane — watch and pray — where Peter did neither and slept. He is not issuing a command he has never failed.

'Your adversary the devil.' Antidikos is a courtroom word: the opponent in a lawsuit, the prosecutor. And that is a precise description of what these readers were experiencing — they were being accused, publicly and continuously.

'Prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.' The picture is hunting, and notice what a roaring lion is doing. A lion stalking prey is silent; the roar comes to panic the herd and drive something out of it. The noise is a weapon, and it works on the nerves rather than the body.

'Seeking someone' — the hunt is selective. He is looking for the one that has drifted from the group, which is exactly what persecution does to a congregation.

'Resist him, firm in your faith.' The command is to stand, not to attack. And 'firm' is a solid word — settled, not moving — which is the opposite of the scattering the roar is designed to produce.

Then the encouragement, and it is unexpectedly practical: 'knowing that the same kinds of suffering are being experienced by your brotherhood throughout the world.' Not a promise of relief but of company. Isolation is the lion's method, and the answer is the knowledge that you are one of many — which is why Peter wrote a circular letter to five provinces rather than a private note.

verseByVerse.quote: And after you have suffered a little while, the God of all grace, who has called you to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you. To him be the dominion forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And after you have suffered a little while.' Peter does not remove the suffering from the sentence. It stands, and it is bounded — a little while, the same phrase as 1:6, measured against the eternal glory in the next clause.

'The God of all grace.' The title is chosen for the moment. Not the God of all power, though he is; the God of all grace — every kind of it, sufficient for every situation these scattered congregations were in.

'Who has called you to his eternal glory in Christ.' The calling looks past the suffering to the destination, and the destination is his own glory. Peter said in verse 1 that he is a partaker of it; here he says they are called to it.

Then four verbs, and they build: 'will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you.'

Restore is the mending word — used of setting a broken bone and of repairing nets, which Peter had done for a living. It assumes damage: the suffering will break something, and God will set it. Confirm means to make firm, the word the Lord used when he told Peter that after turning again he should strengthen his brothers (Luke 22:32). Strengthen is to fill with strength. And establish is to lay on a foundation — to ground something so it cannot be shifted.

And the emphatic word is 'himself'. Not through an agency or a process. God will personally do the mending — which is the promise a battered congregation needed, and it comes from a man who had been broken and repaired by name.

'To him be the dominion forever and ever. Amen.' Peter has just named the prowling lion; he ends by saying whose the dominion actually is.

verseByVerse.quote: By Silvanus, a faithful brother as I regard him, I have written briefly to you, exhorting and declaring that this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it. She who is at Babylon, who is likewise chosen, sends you greetings, and so does Mark, my son. Greet one another with the kiss of love. Peace to all of you who are in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'By Silvanus, a faithful brother as I regard him, I have written briefly to you.' Silvanus is the Silas of Acts — Paul's companion through Philippi and Thessalonica, a Roman citizen, and now carrying Peter's letter. He may have been the letter's scribe as well as its courier, which would account for the polished Greek of a Galilean fisherman.

'Exhorting and declaring that this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it.' That is Peter's own summary of what he has written, and it repays notice. After five chapters on suffering, submission and slander, he calls the whole thing grace. Not advice, not endurance training. Grace — and their part is simply to stand in it.

'She who is at Babylon, who is likewise chosen, sends you greetings.' 'She' is almost certainly the church there, and 'Babylon' is almost certainly Rome. Jewish writers of the period used the name for the great pagan power that had destroyed Jerusalem, and Revelation does the same.

It is a fitting last image for this letter. Peter writes to exiles from the empire's capital and calls it Babylon — the place of exile — reminding them that the church at the centre of the world is as much in a foreign country as the church in Bithynia. And 'likewise chosen' hands them back the word he opened with (1:1).

'And so does Mark, my son.' John Mark — the young man who abandoned Paul and Barnabas, was restored, and by early tradition wrote his Gospel from Peter's preaching. 'My son' is affection, not paternity.

'Greet one another with the kiss of love. Peace to all of you who are in Christ.' The letter that has spoken so much of hostility ends with an instruction to touch each other, and with peace — offered to people who had very little of it, from a man who would shortly die in the city he calls Babylon.
